about_why_h2: Why Is Reorganization Needed Now?<small>なぜ今、再編が必要なのか</small>
issue1_p: As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago. Meanwhile, the population aged 65 and over has increased approximately 2.5 times.
issue2_p: Shinooka Elementary School was built in 1958 (over 60 years ago), and Shinooka Junior High School was built in 1965 (about 60 years ago). Other schools are similarly aging.
issue3_p: If current trends continue, by 2033, all elementary schools and Shinooka Junior High School in the Shinooka area are projected to have only one class per grade.

about_merits_h2: Expected Benefits of Reorganization<small>再編で期待されること</small>
about_merits_intro: Based on official city documents, a parent survey (July 2025, 471 respondents), and discussions at the School Review Meetings, here are the main expected benefits of the school reorganization.
merit1_p: With one class per grade, students spend all 6 years of elementary school and 3 years of junior high with the same classmates. After reorganization, schools will be large enough to reshuffle classes every year, preventing relationships from becoming rigid. 66.4% of parents cited fixed social dynamics as a current concern.
merit2_p: Daily interaction with more classmates creates an environment where children naturally encounter diverse ways of thinking and values. In the parent survey, 52.2% hoped for opportunities to develop independence and teamwork in a group, while 48.6% wanted an environment with more friends.
merit3_p: More students means more clubs, committees, and activities to choose from. This was the #1 expectation (55.2%) among parents in the survey — the top benefit cited for reorganization.
merit4_p: The four reorganized schools will operate as "Shinooka Gakuen" with a unified 9-year curriculum. Stronger elementary–junior high coordination is expected to ease the "middle school transition gap." 46.1% of parents expect improved academic and life guidance through this coordination.
merit5_p: Small schools struggle to maintain a well-balanced mix of experienced and specialist teachers. Larger schools enable better staffing, allowing diverse teaching expertise to be fully utilized.
merit6_p: Shinooka Elementary School was built in 1958 — now 67 years old; Shinooka Junior High in 1965. Reorganization allows the city to carry out planned replacements and provide students with safe, modern learning environments.

about_learn_h2: Learning and Support after the Reorganization<small>再編後の学びと支え</small>
about_learn_lead: A summary of what the city has said in its published material about teaching after the reorganization, classes and teachers, support during the transition, and health and safety. All of it is rewritten by this site from the city's material.
about_learn_c1_p: The city has long practised “learning together” — lessons in which children listen to each other and deepen their learning by accepting each other's ideas. In the city's view this works best with groups large enough to meet a range of ways of thinking and values. At the same time, the city accepts that small schools have the advantage of keeping every child in view.
about_learn_c2_p: The city's optimal size is 12–24 classes per school for both elementary and junior high (2–4 classes per grade in elementary, 4–8 in junior high). The city added to the plan that optimal size means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and that it has no intention of rejecting small classes. The maximum class size is 35 for every elementary grade and the first year of junior high, and 40 for the second and third years; Aichi Prefecture plans to lower the second and third years to 35 in stages from FY2026. The national government also changed the law in 2026, setting the junior high standard at 35 (phased in until FY2027). The city told the city council that a class size of about 21–25 children, large enough to allow classes to be reshuffled, needs to be secured.
about_learn_c3_p: The city says that staff numbers will rise as pupil numbers rise with the reorganization, and that it is working with the prefecture so that staff can be placed as planned for FY2027. Staff numbers at public elementary and junior high schools are calculated from the number of classes under national law (the Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers).
about_learn_c4_p: So that the change does not weigh on children, exchanges between schools are under way before the reorganization (in elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons and an exchange in Tokadai Central Park; in junior high, joint satoyama conservation and arts appreciation by Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High). The city also states that it will publicize and strengthen counselling by each school's counsellors and school counsellors, pass on information and support methods for children who need support, and maintain special-needs classes and resource-room instruction. The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided).
about_learn_c5_h: Where the new schools' content is decided
about_learn_c5_p: Since July 2025 a preparatory research committee has been discussing the new schools' curriculum, educational goals, school song, emblem, clubs and more. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4).
about_learn_c6_p: As a heatstroke measure, the city says it is installing bottle-refill water dispensers in every elementary and junior high school for use from summer 2026 (same, No. 5). By law, elementary and junior high schools have a school nurse-teacher (the health-room teacher) (School Education Act). The gyms and grounds of closing schools are expected to remain in use as evacuation shelters and sites from FY2027 onward.

For Shiroyama 3rd & 4th-chome, a community meeting was held on July 27, 2025, and a resident survey was conducted before finalizing the district boundaries. Procedural details were sent to affected households in June 2026. Note: if a family opts to change its designated school and the commute then exceeds 2 km, the school bus is NOT available.

about_phase2_h2: About Phase 2 Reorganization<small>第2期再編について</small>
about_phase2_box: Outlook after Phase 1: If student numbers continue to decline after Phase 1 (FY2027), further consolidation into 1 elementary and 1 junior high school may be considered, along with the introduction of integrated elementary-junior high education. The decision on Phase 2 will be made based on the situation following Phase 1.
about_phase2_ikkan: What the city says about integrated elementary–junior high education: As advantages, the city lists systematic learning across nine years, easing the stumble on entering junior high, and continuing support suited to each child; as drawbacks, the loss of the break between elementary and junior high, fewer chances for older elementary pupils to develop leadership and independence, and a possible increase in teachers' paperwork. It says it will start with elementary–junior high cooperation and consider a move to integrated education while listening carefully to schools and parents.

faq_q1: OverviewWhy is the reorganization happening in FY2027?
faq_a1:
The city states: "Given the declining number of students, there is no time to delay school reorganization — it must be carried out as soon as possible."

As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago. If current trends continue, by 2033 all elementary schools and Shinooka JHS are projected to have only one class per grade, raising concerns about insufficient numbers for group activities, sports events, and club activities.
faq_a2:
In Phase 1 (FY2027), schools will be reorganized as follows:

[Elementary]
· Tokadai Higashi Elementary ← Shinooka, Hikarigaoka, Oshiro (Okusa & Shiroyama 3-chome)
· Tokadai Nishi Elementary ← Momogaoka, Sue, Oshiro (Shiroyama 2nd/4th/5th-chome)

[Junior High]
· Tokadai Higashi JHS ← Shinooka JHS, Hikarigaoka JHS (except Shiroyama 4-chome)
· Tokadai Nishi JHS ← Toryo JHS, Hikarigaoka JHS (Shiroyama 4-chome)

The Oshiro Elementary district is split depending on the specific neighborhood.
faq_a3: After Phase 1 (FY2027), if student numbers continue to decline, the two elementary schools may be further consolidated into 1 elementary and 1 junior high, introducing integrated elementary-junior high education. The decision on Phase 2 will be based on outcomes of Phase 1.
faq_a4:
School bus service is planned for eligible elementary students in the service area (commuting distance of 2 km or more, etc.) — fully free.

· Morning route: 1 trip

· Cost: Fully covered by the city (free for students)

Note: For Shiroyama 3rd & 4th-chome, if a family opts to change its designated school and the commute then exceeds 2 km, the school bus is NOT available.
faq_q5: CommutingHow will junior high students commute?
faq_a5: Bicycle commuting is planned for junior high students. Details on safe routes and rainy-day arrangements will be studied and announced in due course.
faq_q6: ClubsWhat will happen to extracurricular clubs?
faq_a6: With more students after consolidation, a wider variety of club activities is expected. Currently some clubs cannot run due to low numbers at small schools. After consolidation, students should have more options. Specific clubs will be decided during preparation based on teacher staffing and facilities.
faq_q7: FacilitiesWhat will happen to the buildings of closing schools?
faq_a7:
The school buildings are generally planned to be demolished.
However, gymnasiums and school grounds are generally planned to be kept for local sports and community activities.
faq_q8: CommunityWhat will happen to sports days and community events?
faq_a8: School-run sports days will be held at the consolidated schools. However, community events organized by local neighborhood associations (sports days, summer festivals, etc.) can continue independently. Maintaining links with former school districts' community events after consolidation is a topic for the preparation process.
faq_q9: FacilitiesWhich buildings will the new schools use?
faq_a9: The new schools will use the current buildings of Hikarigaoka Elementary, Momogaoka Elementary, Hikarigaoka JHS, and Toryo JHS respectively. Details on renovations will be studied and announced in due course.
faq_q10: ParticipationHas the public comment period ended?
faq_a10:
Yes. The public comment period ran from November 10 to December 9, 2025, receiving 142 submissions from 55 people (submitters: 39 by email, 13 by fax, 1 by post, 2 in person).

The city has published its responses and a revised plan on the official city website.
faq_q11: ParticipationCan I still share my opinion with the city?
faq_a11:
While the public comment period has closed, you can still share views by phone or in person at the School Reorganization Promotion Division (TEL: 0568-39-5261).

For more details, visit the official city website.
faq_q12: ParticipationIs information available in other languages?
faq_a12: Yes. Issues 1–5 of the "Shinooka School Reorganization Newsletter" have been translated into Spanish, Filipino (Tagalog), Vietnamese, Portuguese, and Chinese. Download them from the official city website. Issue 6 is so far available in Japanese only.
faq_q13: CommuteWhat is being done about safety on the route to school?
faq_a13: Each school inspects its routes every year and responds with signs, green edge lines and similar measures. For the routes after the merger, the city says it will carry out the necessary work once the routes are formally designated, and that the budget for this has been secured. Watching over children is done by route-patrol volunteers; the city notes this is goodwill work and daily cover cannot be promised, and that it will step up recruitment as volunteer numbers fall. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q14: CommuteIs anything being done about walking to school in extreme heat?
faq_a14: The city says heat protection matters regardless of the reorganization, and that recent extreme summers have to be dealt with city-wide. As one measure, it is installing water-bottle refill stations at schools in FY2026. (City's reply in the public comment results)
faq_q15: Getting readyWill the children meet each other before the merger?
faq_a15: Yes. After the public comments, the plan was amended to schedule exchanges and joint activities between the schools beforehand, so children get used to the new setting. On 14 July 2026, Year 4 and Year 5 pupils of the five elementary schools met for a joint exchange event at the East Community Centre, and a joint event for every year group of the five schools is planned for October. The city also says it plans, for the elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons with the Komaki Citizens Cultural Foundation and an exchange event in Tokadai Central Park, and for the junior high schools, joint satoyama (woodland) conservation work and an arts appreciation event for Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High Schools. A "practice commute" is planned for February 2027, in which pupils then in years 1–5 will walk the new route or ride the bus from their designated stop. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings; “Shinooka School Reorganization News” vol.6)
faq_q16: Getting readyWe worry about the effect on third-year students' grades and applications.
faq_a16: Teacher numbers follow a prefectural standard based on the number of classes, so the city says it cannot staff above that standard. Within that limit, it says it will keep working to place teachers from the former schools as evenly as possible. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q17: UniformCan uniforms and school supplies still be used?
faq_a17: The junior high uniform is not changing, so it can be handed down between siblings. The older uniforms (the stand-collar and sailor styles) are also allowed under the rules. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q18: SupportWhat happens to the special-needs classes and the Japanese-language room?
faq_a18: A special-needs class is capped at eight children; above that it becomes two or more classes. As for "Animo", the Japanese-language room at Oshiro Elementary, the city plans to move it elsewhere from FY2027 and will announce the location once decided. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q19: Taking partI could not attend the briefing. Can I read what was said?
faq_a19: For the June 2026 parent briefings, the city has published a summary record of the questions and answers for each venue. The questions and answers submitted on comment sheets, and the opinions and proposals, are published too. All of them are on the city's official pages.
faq_q20: Taking partIs there any explanation for families who are not comfortable in Japanese?
faq_a20: The city acknowledges that although the reorganization newsletter has been translated, it has not reached all the families concerned. It says it will now hand out flyers in plain Japanese and other languages directly through each school, and respond to individual worries. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q21: After schoolWhat happens to the after-school childcare club (gakudō)?
faq_a21: A club is to be set up inside each of the two new elementary schools, Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi, prepared on the expectation that more children will use it. How to apply, which rooms it will use and other details have not been announced yet. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q22: SafetyCan a child who walks to school carry a smartphone?
faq_a22: Bringing smartphones and similar devices to school is not allowed unless there is a special reason, and the city says this rule will stay the same after the reorganization. For children who ride the school bus, an app is being introduced to check boarding and getting off (School bus Q&A). (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q23: UniformWhich school cap should we buy? Can we keep using our current one?
faq_a23:
There is no designated school cap at the new schools. Caps designated by the current schools can still be worn from April 2027.

If you buy a new one, choose something easy to wear every day on the way to and from school. The city suggests three things to look for: ① a brim that blocks direct sunlight, ② easy to put on and take off, ③ a material that does not trap heat. Children starting school from April 2027 will hear more from their school at the new-pupil briefing.

All current school supplies can still be used. Items printed with an old school name (such as tracksuits) will come in a new design when you buy or replace them. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q24: FacilitiesWhen a school closes, will it still be an evacuation shelter?
faq_a24:
The city intends to keep maintaining the gymnasiums and grounds of closing schools from April 2027, because schools are important bases for local sport and disaster preparedness. They are therefore expected to remain designated as evacuation shelters and evacuation sites.

How the school buildings and sites will be used is being considered by the relevant city departments. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
faq_q25: ClassesWill classes get bigger? Will there be more teachers?
faq_a25: In some grades, classes will get bigger. The maximum class size is 35 for every elementary grade and the first year of junior high, and 40 for the second and third years; like Aichi Prefecture, the city plans to lower the second and third years to 35 in stages from FY2026. The national government also changed the law in 2026, setting the junior high standard at 35 (phased in until FY2027). The city says that optimal size means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and told the city council that a class size of about 21–25 children, large enough to allow classes to be reshuffled, needs to be secured (Council Proceedings). As for teachers, the city says staff numbers will rise with pupil numbers, that it is working with the prefecture for FY2027, and that it will run its education so that guidance and care for each child are not neglected. (The city's responses to the public comments; the city's answers at the June 2026 parents' briefings)
faq_q26: SupportIs there emotional support for children as their school changes?
faq_a26: The city recognizes that a big change of environment can weigh on children's minds and bodies. It says it will especially publicize and strengthen counselling by each school's counsellors and school counsellors before and after the reorganization, and pass on information and support methods for children who need support to the new schools. Exchanges so that children can meet before the reorganization are also under way (Q&A on exchanges). The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children who are not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided; Council Proceedings). (The city's responses to the public comments)
faq_q27: Getting readyWho decides the new schools' lessons and educational goals, and when?
faq_a27: A preparatory research committee for the school reorganization was set up in July 2025 and is discussing and deciding what the new schools need — curriculum, educational goals, school song, emblem, club activities and more. At the June 2026 parents' briefings, the new schools' educational goals and school life were explained. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026. The types and number of clubs will be decided during preparations, depending on teacher staffing and facilities after the reorganization. (Revised plan; “Shinooka School Reorganization News” Nos. 4 and 5)

council_s0_h: The March 2026 Session<small>令和8年第1回定例会</small>
council_overview_p: At the 1st Regular Session held in March 2026, 53 bills were deliberated, including bills and a petition related to school reorganization. The ordinance amendment to implement the reorganization plan was passed by majority vote, though some council members voted against it, making for a session with significant debate.

council_ord_desc: This amendment formally establishes in the ordinance the "establishment and abolition of schools" needed to implement the Shinooka reorganization. It establishes Tokadai Higashi Elementary, Tokadai Nishi Elementary, Tokadai Higashi JHS, and Tokadai Nishi JHS, and includes the abolition of schools targeted for reorganization.

council_bus_subtitle: Review of "Shinooka District School Bus Operation" (multi-year commitment)
council_bus_desc: After reorganization, some students will have longer commutes, so school bus service is planned. The committee questioned the details of the operating contract.
council_bus_q1: Please explain the school bus operating contract details and the preparation schedule going forward.
council_bus_a1: A pre-enrollment trial will be conducted early in FY2026, with trial bus rides in FY2026–2027. We will prepare carefully, with consideration for all involved, to ensure a smooth full launch.

council_s3_h: General Questions<small>一般質問での審議</small>
council_gq_intro: Questions were raised from three angles: the public comment results and information sharing with residents, the specific content and rationale of the reorganization plan, and the city's stance toward community feedback.
council_gq_q1: Please explain the trends and key content of public comment submissions and the city's view. Also, what steps will be taken to share information and build community understanding?
council_gq_a1: We have held multiple briefing sessions and gathered opinions from local residents. We will continue working to deepen understanding of the plan.
council_gq_q2: The reorganization splits school districts in ways that seem to conflict with community realities. Please explain the plan's rationale and whether it truly fits the local situation.
council_gq_a2: This consolidates elementary schools in Shinooka. Due to declining student numbers, we are reorganizing to create an environment where children can learn alongside diverse peers. We need class sizes of around 21–25 students. School buses are planned for students with longer commutes, with broad coverage as most of Shinooka faces distance challenges.
council_gq_q3: (Follow-up) Many public comments called for review or halt of the plan. How do you view this? Have community views been adequately incorporated?
council_gq_a3: We have responded carefully to all submissions. Rather than rushing, we will proceed with full information disclosure. Our mission is to establish a stable educational environment for children as soon as possible.
council_warn_title: ⚠️ Issue Highlighted in General Questions: Public Comment Assessment
council_warn_p: It was pointed out that a high proportion of public comments called for the plan to be "reviewed or halted", raising questions about the adequacy of the city's response. The city replied it had "responded carefully" and would "proceed with full transparency," maintaining its pro-reorganization stance.

council_s6_h: The June 2026 Session<small>令和8年第2回定例会</small>
council_s6_lead: The session ran 24 days, from 1 to 24 June 2026, and dealt with 26 items including four ordinance bills. None concerned the school reorganization, and nothing was voted down. Only the amendment to the municipal tax ordinance split the chamber; everything else passed unanimously.
council_r2_intro: Two questions were asked: how the city views the option of keeping small schools, and what the buildings of closed schools will be used for.
council_r2_q1: The national government (MEXT) says keeping small schools is also an option. Is that only for depopulated areas and remote islands? Which areas does it cover?
council_r2_a1: It is not limited to particular areas; each area's own circumstances have to be taken into account. However, the circumstances of depopulated areas and of the Shinooka district are very different.
council_r2_q2: How does the city view the option of keeping a small school where the community needs it?
council_r2_a2: From the standpoint of securing a better learning environment for children, we will consider it based on the city-wide school plan, taking local circumstances into account.
council_r2_q3: Is it right to understand that the Board of Education intends to make use of closed school facilities, classrooms included?
council_r2_a3: We are considering opening a comprehensive education support centre for children who do not attend school, and using a closed school building is one of the candidates. However, no policy has been decided yet.
council_r2_q4: When considering the use of school facilities, will only educational facilities such as that centre be considered, or other kinds of facilities as well?
council_r2_a4: We will first set a direction for the city as a whole and then proceed. Not limited to educational facilities, we will make an overall judgement that also takes in location, land use and facility management.
council_r2_other_title: 🧒 A question listed by title only: after-school childcare clubs in Shinooka
council_r2_other_p: Another general question was titled “After-school childcare clubs in the Shinooka district”. The newsletter gives only the title, not the question or the answer. If you want to know what was said, ask the Council Secretariat's Proceedings Division (contact details at the bottom of this page).
council_r2_visit_h: Committee Study Visit<small>委員会の行政調査</small>
council_r2_visit_title: 🔍 Education and Construction Committee: a compulsory education school in Soja, Okayama (18 May)
council_r2_visit_p1: Newsletter No. 215 also reports a study visit the Education and Construction Committee made ahead of the June session. On 18 May the committee visited Soja City in Okayama Prefecture, which runs compulsory education schools, and looked at how Showa Itsutsuboshi Gakuen became one, its features and current situation, and its outlook.
council_r2_visit_p2: In its findings the committee notes that Komaki, too, is looking ahead to setting up “integrated-type elementary and junior high schools” as part of its 9-year integrated education, and concludes that schools, the PTA, parents and the community need to keep talking this through together for the sake of future pupils.
council_r2_next: 3rd Regular Session (Aug–Oct): According to the notice in Newsletter No. 215, the 3rd Regular Session was scheduled from 25 August to 5 October, with general questions on 2–4 September and the Education and Construction Committee on 9 September. For the outcome, see the City Council’s own announcements.
council_quality_h: Answers on the Quality of Education<small>教育の質に関わる答弁</small>
council_quality_lead: From the answers and reports on this page, three concern children's learning and growth. Nothing here is new — it gathers points from the sections above.
council_quality_l1: Class size: In general questions at the March session, the city answered that, so that children can push each other to grow among a variety of classmates, a class size of about 21–25 children, large enough to allow classes to be reshuffled, needs to be secured. See the answer ↑
council_quality_l2: Support for children not attending school: In general questions at the June session, the city answered that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for such children, with closed school buildings as one candidate site. Nothing has been decided yet. See the answer ↑
council_quality_l3: Integrated elementary–junior high education: The education and construction committee studied a compulsory education school in Soja, Okayama, and concluded that since Komaki is also looking toward integrated elementary–junior high schools, schools, the PTA, parents and the community need to keep talking together. See the report ↑
council_quality_more: What the city has said about learning and support after the reorganization is on About the Plan, and this site's own review and proposals are on Review & ideas (this site's review is not the view of the city or the council).

To put a view to the council directly there are petitions (which need a councillor's endorsement) and representations, and the proceedings are compiled as minutes. All of these are handled by the Proceedings and Research Section of the council secretariat, so asking them is the surest route (contact below). The results are also summarized in the quarterly "Komaki City Council News" (No.214, 1 May 2026 for the March session; No.215, 1 August 2026 for the June session).

voices_pc_h: What the Public Comments Said<small>パブリックコメントで実際に言われたこと</small>
voices_pc_lead: The material in this section comes from the comments the city actually published. The public comment period of 10 November to 9 December 2025 drew 142 submissions from 55 people, and the city published each comment together with its own response. This site read them and summarized them by topic.
voices_pc_themes_h: What the Comments Raised<small>寄せられた意見の論点</small>
voices_pc_themes_lead: The city answered every comment and gave each answer a topic heading of its own. This site counted those headings: 143 of them across 53 topics (the city states 142 comments in total). The eight most frequent are shown here.
pc_th_other: A further 69 headings fall under 45 other topics (1–4 each).
voices_pc_themes_note: Note: a count is not a measure of support or opposition. One person raising several topics is counted once per topic. The categories are the city's own headings; this site only counted them.
voices_pc_q1: "Starting in FY2027 is too soon. Talking it through matters more than meeting a deadline."
voices_pc_a1: The number of children aged 0–5 is already known, so the next six years can be projected quite accurately. Given how fast that number falls, there is no time to spare, and FY2027 is the earliest the change can be made.
voices_pc_q2: "It is moving ahead without enough notice to residents or their agreement. Take it back to the drawing board."
voices_pc_a2: Work on the city-wide school plan began in FY2023 and was explained at town meetings in FY2024. In FY2025 the city set up the local "group to think about the schools" and held parent discussion meetings and public briefings.
voices_pc_q3: "Do not merge schools mechanically to hit a 12-class figure. Smaller classes give children more attention."
voices_pc_a3: "Appropriate size" refers to the number of classes, not the number of children in one class. The city is not against small classes. But where most years have only one class, pupils cannot be reshuffled and relationships become fixed.
voices_pc_q4: "The school is the centre of the neighbourhood. Lose it and the events, the disaster response and the community itself weaken."
voices_pc_a4: A school has many roles, but first of all it is an educational facility. The gym and the grounds are to be kept in principle as community facilities; the classroom buildings will in principle be demolished. Ties with the community are to be deepened through how the new schools are run.
voices_pc_q5: "Walking children through this heat is dangerous, and we worry about safety checks on the bus."
voices_pc_a5: The plan was amended to add a boarding-check system that lets parents and the school confirm a child got on, and a system to prevent children being left on board. On heat, the city treats it as a city-wide issue and is installing water-bottle refill stations at schools in FY2026, among other measures.
voices_pc_mh: What the comments changed in the plan
voices_pc_m1: The foreword now states that a certain school size has to be secured as the birthrate falls
voices_pc_m2: The section on appropriate size now says it means the number of classes, not class size, and that small classes are not being rejected
voices_pc_m3: Boarding checks and a system to prevent children being left on board were added as bus safety measures
voices_pc_m4: The first-phase actions now include planned exchanges and joint activities between schools before the merger
voices_pc_m5: The wording on combined primary-and-lower-secondary education and the second phase changed from "will introduce" to "will study introducing"
voices_pc_note: Both the comments and the city's responses are summaries rewritten by this site, not the original wording. The city publishes the originals on its page for the consultation on the draft Shinooka school reorganization plan.
voice_for1: "If we leave things as they are, by 2033 every school will have just one class per grade. To create an environment where children can learn alongside diverse peers, moving ahead with consolidation now is necessary."
voice_for2: "I was surprised to hear Shinooka Elementary was built in 1958. Sending my child to a 60-year-old building honestly worries me. I support using the reorganization as an opportunity to update the facilities."
voice_for3: "At the current small school, there are few club options and my child had to give up their preferred sport. I'm hopeful that merging into the new schools will open up more choices. The free school bus is also a big help."
voice_for4: "At small schools, teachers often juggle multiple subjects, making specialized instruction difficult. With a properly sized school, teachers can focus on their expertise and lesson quality should improve."
voice_for5: "The population over 65 in the Shinooka area has grown 2.5 times in 20 years while children have halved. There are limits to maintaining multiple small schools. Considering the financial burden on future generations, consolidation is unavoidable."
voice_for6: "As this area has many families with foreign roots, multilingual newsletters are a positive step. An appropriately sized school would bring together children with diverse backgrounds, creating a better educational environment."
voice_against1: "It's dangerous for young children to commute far. Even with a school bus, a long walk to the stop defeats the purpose. Deciding on consolidation before specific safety measures have been presented seems rushed."
voice_against2: "Schools are more than educational facilities — they are the heart of the community. If Shinooka and Momogaoka Elementary disappear, those neighborhoods lose their sports day and festival venues, potentially accelerating community decline."
voice_against3: "Precisely because class sizes are small, teachers can give each child individual attention. The personalized instruction at small schools like Sue Elementary will inevitably be lost as the school grows. Bigger does not equal better education."
voice_against4: "When students suddenly double after consolidation, large-school problems emerge. During my teaching career, I witnessed many times how bullying becomes more complex and children get lost in the crowd."
voice_against5: "Shinooka Junior High has nurtured the children of this community for many years. If the building is old, renovate it. Is it acceptable to close a school with such history so easily? Demolishing the buildings is also deeply sad."
voice_against6: "Currently my child's school is a 5-minute walk, so I can easily drop by as a parent. If the school is far, my involvement will decrease and it will be harder to know what's happening with my child."
voice_against7: "I object to the name 'Shinooka Gakuen.' Using the name of an existing school as the umbrella name for the four new schools feels inconsistent. If the reorganization is a new start, shouldn't the name reflect the diverse history of the broader eastern area?"
voice_neutral1: "I appreciate the city fully covering school bus costs. However, I'd like specific plans — bus stop locations, departure times, bad weather procedures — presented as soon as possible before forming my opinion."
voice_neutral2: "I hope a system can be created so the new schools coordinate with local community events (sports days, summer festivals) in each neighborhood. Even as school structure changes, I hope community bonds are protected."
voice_neutral3: "I'd like the city's responses to the 142 public comments released in a more accessible way. Reading PDFs is difficult for the general public. A plain-language explanation of the revised plan would be appreciated."
voice_neutral4: "Phase 2 envisions consolidating to 1 elementary and 1 junior high with integrated education. Please verify whether Phase 1 truly improves the educational environment before deciding on Phase 2."
voice_neutral5: "Publishing the reorganization newsletter in Spanish, Filipino, Vietnamese, and other languages was a good step. But I hope interpretation at information sessions and multilingual submission options will also be made available."
index_whatis_p1: In the Shinooka area of eastern Komaki City, rapid population decline and aging school facilities have become serious challenges. As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago, and if current trends continue, it is projected that by 2033 all elementary schools and Shinooka Junior High School will have only one class per grade.
index_whatis_p2: In response to this situation, Komaki City has formulated this reorganization plan, viewing the entire Shinooka area as a unified learning community to enrich nine years of continuous education. The four post-reorganization schools will be collectively called "Shinooka Gakuen." The plan aims to consolidate the current 5 elementary and 3 junior high schools into 2 elementary and 2 junior high schools in FY2027.

bus_p: School buses will be introduced for elementary school students who will face longer commutes due to the school reorganization starting in FY2027 (April 2027). The city covers all costs — students ride free.
bus_stats_intro: These three points form the backbone of the school bus plan. See the sections below for details on service areas, safety measures, and registration.
bus_ov_day_p: Operates on school days. Service is suspended during long vacations but runs on school event days such as sports day and term start days.
bus_ov_trips_p:
Morning: 1 trip (all grades)
Afternoon: up to 3 trips (lower grades / upper grades / after extracurricular activities)
bus_ov_free_p: Free for students. The city covers all costs in consideration of the longer commutes resulting from the reorganization.
bus_ov_apply_p: Students in the service area register to use the bus. Capacity and group assignments are reviewed each school year.
bus_area_criteria_p:
Children with a one-way commute of 2 km or more, and areas where local conditions such as significant elevation changes apply, are eligible.
Note: For Shiroyama 3rd & 4th-chome, if a family opts to change its designated school and the commute then exceeds 2 km, the school bus is NOT available.
bus_area_east_p: Ikenouchi, Hayashi, Noguchi, Oyama, and Okusa districts
bus_area_outside: ※ Children outside the service area may be recommended by the Board of Education to use the bus if they are significantly far from the nearest school walking group and group commuting is extremely difficult.
bus_area_pending: ⚠️ The stops, the timetable and the rules of use are being collected in the “School Bus Use Guidelines”, which the city has said will be handed out and explained at the briefing for eligible families. Check the official city page for the briefing dates and the latest information.
bus_timeline_h2: Introduction Timeline<small>導入スケジュール</small>
bus_tl1_body: Contract signed with the operator. Aoi Kotsu Co., Ltd. won the selective tender.
bus_tl2_body: Applications and the user briefing. Forms were posted to households in the service area; they were accepted 30 Aug – 30 Sep (now closed).
bus_tl3_body: Trial rides and app testing. Preparation proceeds step by step while the actual routes and stops are checked.
bus_safety_check_p: A system will be introduced to allow parents and schools to confirm in real time that their child has boarded the bus.
bus_safety_left_p: A system will be installed to prevent children from being left behind on the bus, ensuring safety after boarding.
bus_safety_guide_p: The city intends to put an attendant on every school bus (newsletter vol.4). Attendants are hired through an outside contractor. At the June 2026 briefings the city said their three duties are running the boarding-check app, helping children on and off, and contacting the school and other bodies in an accident or emergency.
bus_faq_h2: Frequently Asked Questions<small>よくある質問</small>
bus_faq_q1: BoardingWhat if my child misses the bus?
bus_faq_a1: If a child misses the bus, the app sends a notice and the school also gets in touch; as a rule the family is asked to handle it. The city says the bus cannot turn back, because that would upset the timetable. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_q2: EmergenciesWhat happens during typhoons or weather warnings?
bus_faq_a2: What happens when a weather warning is issued will be set out in the “School Bus Use Guidelines”. It is expected to follow the school’s own decision on whether to open.
bus_faq_q3: AreaCan children outside the service area ride the bus?
bus_faq_a3: Eligibility is decided by home address. The city says the covered area has been stretched as far as the bus capacity allows, and children outside it are asked to walk. Where a child cannot walk because of a disability or similar, the city will consider the case individually with the school and the operator. Where the bus leaves a walking group too small, groups will be merged with neighbouring ones. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_a4: Yes. The city covers all costs because the reorganization increases commute distances for these students. There is no charge for students or families.
bus_faq_q5: Bus StopsWhere will the bus stops be?
bus_faq_a5: The city designates the stops. They were chosen mainly on public land, with the safety of waiting children first and with account taken of where children live. Children are expected to walk to the stop as a group, using the existing walking groups. The exact stops and timetable are to be given at the briefings for eligible families. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_q6: RegistrationWhen and how do we apply?
bus_faq_a6: In August 2026 the application form and a briefing invitation were posted to guardians of children inside the service area. The deadline was 30 August – 30 September, and the form had to be returned whether or not a seat was wanted. Applications closed on 30 September. See how to apply.
bus_faq_q7: ServiceHow many runs a day, and how long is the ride?
bus_faq_a7: There is one run in the morning and up to three in the afternoon (after period 5, after period 6, and after club activities). A ride is expected to take at most about 20 minutes, and even the earliest meeting time is to be kept no earlier than 7:20. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_q8: SafetyIs an adult on board with the children?
bus_faq_a8: Yes, an attendant rides along. The city says it had not planned one at first, but added the role after hearing worries about a child being alone with the driver and requests for help boarding. The attendant helps children on and off, watches over the cabin and responds in emergencies; the role will be filled through an outside contract. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_q9: SafetyCan parents check that their child got on the bus?
bus_faq_a9: The plan now includes a boarding-check system that lets parents and the school confirm the child got on safely, plus a system to prevent a child being left on board. The city is looking at an ICT-based checking tool and says it will inform parents once the details are fixed. (City's reply in the public comment results) Later, at the June 2026 briefings, the city explained that the bus attendant operates a boarding-check app used with boarding cards, and that parents are notified through the app if a child misses the bus.
bus_faq_q10: StopsHow were the bus stop locations decided?
bus_faq_a10: Stops were chosen mainly on public land, putting the safety of waiting children first and taking account of where the children live. As a result, the city says, some stops ended up near the edge of the covered area. Children are expected to walk to the stop as a group, using the existing walking groups. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
bus_faq_q11: Bus StopsWill the bus stops have a sign?
bus_faq_a11: No. The city says it will not put up signs, for crime-prevention reasons: marking a spot as a stop would let outsiders know that children gather there at set times. The city assigns each household the stop it will use. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
comm_def_p1: A Community Council is an organization voluntarily formed by local residents based on the elementary school district. Groups such as neighborhood associations, PTAs, senior clubs, sports clubs, and welfare commissioners participate across organizational lines to discuss local issues and revitalize community life.
comm_def_p2: In Komaki City, Community Councils have been established in 14 of the city's 16 elementary school districts (as of April 2026). The five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area (Shinooka, Hikarigaoka, Oshiro, Momogaoka, and Sue) each have their own council.
comm_card_list: 📋 The five Community Councils of the Shinooka area
comm_list_intro: All five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area have a Community Council, and all five were certified by the city on April 1, 2020. The oldest, Sue Elementary District, was founded in 2014 and has over a decade of activity behind it.
comm_list_note:
Note: Each council publishes an annual activity plan and budget on the city website (the FY2026 documents are currently posted). Source: Komaki City, "Establishment and activities of Community Councils" (updated June 4, 2026). Representatives' names are personal information and are not reproduced here.
For the latest information and details on each council, see the city's Community Council page.
comm_act_intro: Community Councils carry out a wide range of activities that span generations.
comm_act_list:
• Disaster preparedness & safety: Organizing and participating in area-wide disaster drills, preparing evacuation-shelter manuals, disaster imagination games (DIG)
  • Crime prevention: Forming blue-light patrol teams, creating safety maps, watching over children
  • Children's events: Kite-flying, mochi-pounding, walk rallies, sports meets, and more
  • Community exchange: Summer festivals, fireworks shows, music festivals
  • Senior support: Wellness salons, Orange Cafés (dementia cafés), neighbourhood helper teams
  • Digital support: Smartphone classes
comm_act_note: The city groups local issues into four areas — disaster preparedness, crime prevention, welfare, and exchange — and each council plans its projects along these lines.
comm_base_p: As the name "○○ Elementary School District" implies, the elementary school district is the geographic foundation of each Community Council. School districts serve as units of social cohesion, and Community Councils use this framework to cultivate horizontal connections among residents.
comm_cs_p1: Each school in Komaki City has a School Management Council (Community School). This is a forum where parents and local residents can share opinions on the school's educational policies and operations — an important institution connecting Community Councils with schools.
comm_cs_p2: It creates opportunities for local adults to participate in classroom support, read-alouds, and career education, and to share school challenges with the wider community.
comm_fac_p: The gymnasiums, sports fields, and pools of each school are used daily by local residents for community sports and as disaster bases (evacuation sites). Community members also participate in school events such as sports meets and learning fairs, making schools serve as the public "face" of the community.
comm_club_p: After-school childcare clubs for children of dual-income families are also organized on a school-district basis and operate in coordination with Community Councils and PTAs. After the reorganization, a club is to be set up inside each of Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi elementary schools (FAQ).
comm_row1_after: To be reorganized into 2 councils; transition to new structure planned for FY2029. Specific groupings are currently under review.
comm_row2_after: Will be newly organized in each of the 4 new schools after reorganization. (From official Komaki City Q&A, Q11)
comm_row3_after: Even after consolidation, gymnasiums and sports grounds of closed schools will in principle be retained as "important community bases for local sports and disaster preparedness."
comm_row4_after: Placement by school district will continue. After the reorganization, clubs are to be set up inside Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi elementary schools.
comm_row5_after: Consolidation will expand the activity area. Continuity of existing events and activities will be decided through discussions within each council and community.
comm_qa1_q: What will happen to current activities when the councils are reduced to two?
comm_qa1_a: The city has announced a policy of reorganizing to 2 Community Councils by FY2029, but how the integration proceeds and how each event will be handled will be determined through consultations with residents and the individual councils. At this point, many details about how activities will be handed over remain undecided, and it is hoped that a forum will be provided for residents' voices to be reflected.
comm_qa2_q: Won't community bonds weaken if the local school disappears?
comm_qa2_a: Schools have served as hubs for community events, disaster preparedness, sports, and childcare. School consolidation means the number of these hubs will change, but the city has declared a policy of continuing community use of closed school facilities, so gymnasiums and sports fields are expected to remain available. How to rebuild the community itself will need to be discussed with residents taking the lead.
comm_qa3_q: Will Community School activities disappear with the school consolidation?
comm_qa3_a: They won't disappear. New School Management Councils (Community Schools) will be organized in each of the 4 new schools after reorganization (Tokadai Higashi Elementary, Tokadai Nishi Elementary, Tokadai Higashi Junior High, Tokadai Nishi Junior High). However, how to carry on the relationships and activities cultivated by each current school's Community School depends on future consultations. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4).
comm_qa4_q: What will happen to local events that each community has independently continued?
comm_qa4_a: Events that each Community Council has organized over many years (disaster drills, children's events, local festivals, etc.) are activities carried out by local residents. Even after the councils are integrated, continuation is possible based on the will and consensus of local residents, but the specific form will be at the discretion of the new post-reorganization councils. No official policy has yet been announced.

comm_sec5_disclaimer: ※ This section summarizes points commonly raised when community organizations based on school districts are merged. How it will actually proceed in the Shinooka district will be decided through discussions between the city and each council.
comm_consider1:
Schools and community ties
Schools bring together not only children but also parents and local residents. Events such as sports days, school presentations and evacuation drills are also occasions for people of different generations to meet. For this reason, school mergers are often described as affecting not only the learning environment but also how local people are connected.
comm_consider2:
Points raised when organizations cover a wider area
A wider area can make it easier to pool people and funds, and lets residents across a larger area work together. On the other hand, taking part can become harder once activities go beyond the circle of people who know each other, and attachment to the former school district may fade. Which side comes out stronger is generally said to depend on how the transition is handled and how residents take part.
comm_consider3:
How the transition proceeds
When local organizations merge, the timing, how activities are handed over, and how residents are informed and consulted become the main issues. In the Shinooka district, the five councils are to be reorganized into two, targeting fiscal 2029, and how the merger proceeds will be decided through future discussions. At the 2025 briefings and public comment process, residents also voiced concern about the future of the local community.

nationwide_p: School reorganization is not happening only in eastern Komaki. By placing the national standards and nationwide statistics side by side, this page shows where this plan sits.
nationwide_source_intro: Sources: Every figure and standard on this page comes from materials published by MEXT (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology). For the Komaki plan itself, see Plan Overview.
nationwide_s1_h: Nationwide in Numbers<small>数字でみる全国</small>
nationwide_s1_lead: School consolidation driven by the falling birthrate has continued across Japan for decades. These are the nationwide closure figures from MEXT surveys.
nationwide_stat1_l: public schools closed nationwide over the 20 years from FY2004 to FY2023
nationwide_stat2_l: schools closed in FY2023 alone (191 elementary, 82 junior high, 25 high school and other)
nationwide_stat3_l: closures in Aichi Prefecture over the same 20 years (62 elementary, 14 junior high, 16 other)
nationwide_stat4_l: of the 7,612 closed school buildings still standing are being used for another purpose
nationwide_s1_note: The number of public elementary and junior high schools fell by about 2,000 in roughly ten years, and the number of pupils by about 850,000.
nationwide_s2_h: What the National Standards Say<small>国が示している基準</small>
nationwide_s2_lead: The national government sets guideline figures for school size and commuting conditions. All of them are flexible — "unless there are special circumstances" — and each municipality decides for itself what to actually do.
nationwide_row1_national: 12 to 18 classes is the standard for elementary and junior high schools; 18 to 27 for compulsory education schools.
nationwide_row1_komaki: On the current trend, every elementary school and Shinooka JHS would have just one class per grade by 2033.
nationwide_row2_national: Roughly within 4 km for elementary and 6 km for junior high (the condition for national subsidy).
nationwide_row2_komaki: School buses for elementary pupils commuting 2 km or more, fully funded by the city (free of charge).
nationwide_row3_national: Where transport is used, roughly one hour or less is the rough guideline.
nationwide_row3_komaki: Stops and timetable to be set in the “School Bus Use Guidelines” and shown at the briefing for eligible families.
nationwide_row4_national: 35 in elementary school. Junior high also became 35 under a 2026 change in the law, phased in grade by grade until FY2027.
nationwide_row4_komaki: 35 for every elementary grade and the first year of junior high; the second and third years move to 35 in stages from FY2026, as in Aichi Prefecture. The city says optimal size means the number of classes, not the number of children per class.
nationwide_row5_national: Calculated from the number of classes.
nationwide_row5_komaki: Staff numbers rise with pupil numbers; the city is working with the prefecture for FY2027.
nationwide_s2_note: The national figures come from Articles 41, 49 and 79-3 of the Enforcement Regulations of the School Education Act, and Article 4 of the Enforcement Order of the Act on National Treasury Subsidies for School Facilities. For Komaki's own commuting plan, see the School Bus page. Class size and teacher numbers follow the Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers of Public Compulsory Education Schools, Articles 3 and 7, and the supplementary provisions of Act No. 7 of 2026.
nationwide_s3_h: August 2026: National Guidance Revised for the First Time in Ten Years<small>2026年8月、国の手引が10年ぶりに改訂</small>
nationwide_s3_lead: MEXT has revised, for the first time in ten years, the guidance municipalities use when reviewing school size and placement. The revision has three main points.
nationwide_s3_c1_p: Rather than looking only within its own boundaries, a municipality should consider the wider area including neighbouring municipalities. Schools jointly established by several municipalities are given as an example.
nationwide_s3_c2_p: Not only the board of education but the mayor's departments too should treat this as a question about the area's future, considered together with transport provision and town planning.
nationwide_s3_c3_p: The text is updated for the revised curriculum guidelines and for learning that assumes one device per pupil, including linking small schools to each other online.
nationwide_s3_basic:
• Improving educational conditions for children is the centre of any review.
  • Each municipality decides for itself.
  • Whether schools are merged or kept, the benefits must be used and the drawbacks minimized.
nationwide_s3_quote: New wording on building consensus: The revision adds the importance of "careful, dialogue-based discussion" and of setting "a timeline that does not keep postponing a conclusion." It states that the process matters — not merely asking whether to merge, but having everyone involved discuss what a school is for and how they want children to grow.
nationwide_s3_bus: On school buses: Because the shortage of drivers is affecting local public transport as a whole, the revision states that municipalities considering buses should work with the mayor's departments to secure transport for the area as a whole.
nationwide_s4_h: School Size and Pupil Numbers Nationwide<small>全国の学校規模と子どもの数</small>
nationwide_s4_lead: The situation troubling eastern Komaki — close to one class per grade — is happening at many schools across Japan.
nationwide_s4_list:
• About 40% of public elementary schools and about 50% of public junior high schools have fewer than 12 classes.
  • About 16% of municipalities are down to a single elementary school and a single junior high school — some 60 more than a decade ago.
  • Elementary pupils number 5,812,000 and junior high students 3,105,000, both record lows (as of 1 May 2025).
nationwide_s4_note: Sources: MEXT "Outline of the Revised Guidance" (August 2026) and the FY2025 School Basic Survey (final figures).
nationwide_s5_h: The Combined Elementary–Junior High Option<small>小中一貫という形</small>
nationwide_s5_p: Under the eastern Komaki plan, a second phase merging down to one elementary and one junior high school with combined elementary–junior high education is also being considered. Nationwide there were 232 public compulsory education schools — a single school covering both levels — in FY2024, with 75,828 pupils; enrolment reached a record 87,000 in FY2025. The statutory standard size is 18 to 27 classes.
nationwide_s5_link: See what is being considered for Phase 2 →
nationwide_s5b_h: The Combined Junior–Senior High Option<small>中高一貫という形</small>
nationwide_s5b_p:
Combined junior–senior high school education, which links the six years of junior high and senior high, became part of the system in April 1999. It takes three forms:
  • Secondary education schools: a single school teaching all six years as one. 57 schools (4 national, 35 public, 18 private)
  • Attached type: a junior high and a senior high run by the same body, linked with no senior-high entrance exam. 537 schools (1 national, 105 public, 431 private)
  • Partnership type: possible even between different bodies; the schools cooperate on curriculum and on exchanges of teachers and pupils. 84 schools (79 public, 5 private)
That makes 678 schools in FY2023, a number that has kept rising since the system began. About 80% of the attached type are private; nearly all of the partnership type are public.
nationwide_s5b_note: Sources: MEXT, “Overview and status of combined junior–senior high school education”; reference material 5 for the 14th meeting of the Working Group on the Future of Senior High School Education (12 September 2024), with figures from the School Basic Survey.

The state issues guidance; each municipality decides.</dd><dt>Compulsory education school</dt><dd>A single school covering elementary and junior high, able to run one nine-year curriculum.</dd><dt>Combined junior–senior high education</dt><dd>Teaching the six years of junior and senior high as one continuous course.
