rev_h1: Reviewing the plan, and what could come next
rev_p: We have condensed what this site has examined into 10 key findings, and our proposals — for protecting and raising the quality of education and for increasing the number of children in the eastern district — into 10 key proposals. The evidence for each can be read in detail on the In-depth review page.
rev_stance: ⚠️ This page contains this site’s own review and proposals. They are not the position of Komaki City or its Board of Education. Anything marked 【Fact】 comes from published material and is sourced, while anything marked 🔎 review or 💡 proposal is this site’s own thinking. Please read the two separately. Views for and against the plan are on Voices, and the national picture and standards are on Nationwide.
rev_stance_general: Note that the 🔎 reviews and 💡 proposals reason from general grounds — how the rules work and what other places have done — on top of the published material. This site has no inside information about the district.
rev_s1_h: The numbers this review rests on<small>検証の土台になる数字</small>
rev_s1_lead: The review below rests on the published figures listed here. All of them come from Komaki City’s official information or from statistics published by MEXT.
rev_f1_v: As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka district is less than half what it was 20 years ago; the population aged 65 and over is about 2.5 times larger
rev_f2_v: By 2033 every elementary school in the district, and Shinooka Junior High, is expected to have only one class per year group
rev_f3_v: In FY2027, five elementary and three junior high schools become two elementary and two junior high schools
rev_f4_v: If numbers fall further, merging into one elementary and one junior high school with integrated 9-year education is under consideration; the decision is to be made after seeing how Phase 1 goes
rev_f5_v: Held 10 November – 9 December 2025; 142 submissions from 55 people in total (submitters: 39 by e-mail, 13 by fax, 1 by post, 2 in person)
rev_f6_v: Covers children living 2 km or more from school, plus areas set with local conditions in mind. Expected users: about 100 in Tokadai Nishi and about 160 in Tokadai Higashi
rev_src_letter: Shinooka District School Reorganization Newsletter vol. 3
rev_f7_v: Aoi Kotsu Co. won the tender at 111,750,000 yen (before tax); the contract runs from 8 June 2026 to 31 March 2030
rev_f8_v: Five councils are to become two, targeted for FY2029. How the merger will work is still to be discussed
rev_f9_v: 12 to 18 classes is the standard for elementary and junior high schools. About 40% of public elementary schools and about 50% of junior high schools nationwide are below 12 classes
rev_f10_v: Revised on 5 August 2026 for the first time in ten years. Its three pillars are wider-area, whole-of-government and modernised thinking, and it asks municipalities to consider schools together with town planning
rev_f11_k: The prefecture's integrated junior/senior high schools
rev_f11_v: Aichi opened four prefectural integrated junior/senior high schools in April 2025 and six more in April 2026. Each attaches a new junior high to an existing prefectural high school; only Miwa High School uses the co-operative type, working with municipal junior highs (Aichi's policy on introducing integrated education)
rev_f12_v: The number of junior high graduates is expected to fall by about 20% by FY2035. The prefecture is consolidating its high schools: in FY2028 four schools in the Seto area become three (Prefectural High School Reorganization Vision)
rev_s1_note: The detail behind these figures, with source links, is on About the plan, School bus and Nationwide. For official information, see the Komaki City Board of Education page.
rev_s2_h: 🔎 Review: what the plan does not say<small>検証：計画から読み取れないこと</small>
rev_s2_lead: Six points that could not be confirmed from the published material. The question is not whether the plan is right, but whether the information needed to judge it is there. ① and ④ concern the forecast and the criteria for decisions, ③ and ⑥ the boundary and the buildings, and ② and ⑤ the way the process is run.
rev_i1_h: 1. The assumptions behind “one class per year by 2033” are not shown
rev_i1_f: 【Fact】The city states that “given the decline in the number of children there is no time to spare, and the reorganization must be carried out as soon as possible”, and expects every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High to have one class per year group by 2033.
rev_i1_v: 🔎 Our view: Only the result of the projection has been published. The assumptions behind it — births, families moving in and out, new housing — are not in any published material we could find. If they were shown, residents could tell apart what cannot be changed from what policy could still change.
rev_i2_h: 2. Nothing in the plan works on increasing the number of children
rev_i2_f: 【Fact】The published plan is built around reorganizing schools. The national guidance revised in August 2026 sets out a “whole-of-government” pillar, asking that the mayoral departments as well as the board of education consider schools together with transport and town planning.
rev_i2_v: 🔎 Our view: Reorganization responds to the fall in the number of children; responding to the fall itself — housing, childcare, transport — sits with other departments. The published material does not show the two being considered in the same place.
rev_i3_h: 3. It is hard to see why the eligibility line falls where it does
rev_i3_f: 【Fact】The school bus covers children who live 2 km or more away, plus areas set with local conditions in mind. However, for Shiroyama 3-chome and 4-chome, children are not covered even if the change of school district takes their journey past 2 km. The city has said the guidelines setting stops, timetables and rules are to be handed out at briefings; applications were accepted from 30 August to 30 September 2026.
rev_i3_v: 🔎 Our view: The same 2 km can mean covered in one case and not covered in another, and the reason is not easy to read out of the published material. The application deadline also falls before the content of the guidelines is settled.
rev_i4_h: 4. There is no stated test for moving to Phase 2
rev_i4_f: 【Fact】Phase 2 — merging into one elementary and one junior high school with integrated 9-year education — is to be considered “if the number of children falls further after Phase 1”, with the decision made in the light of how Phase 1 goes.
rev_i4_v: 🔎 Our view: What level “falls further” refers to is not stated. Unless it is said in advance how Phase 1 will be judged, Phase 2 reads as a route already fixed.
rev_i5_h: 5. How should the consultation process be judged?
rev_i5_f: 【Fact】The public comment drew 142 submissions from 55 people. In the city assembly’s general questions, the high share of submissions calling for the plan to be reviewed or halted became a point of debate. The revised national guidance newly adds both “careful, dialogue-based discussion” and a timeline that “does not put off reaching a conclusion”.
rev_i5_v: 🔎 Our view: Fifty-five people is not a large number against the population of the district, and the count alone cannot measure support or opposition. What matters is not how many replied but how the process was designed: who was reached, and at which stage anything could still change.
rev_i6_h: 6. There is no decided use for the buildings after closure
rev_i6_f: 【Fact】What happens to the closing schools is described in published material as a matter for later consideration. Nationwide, 74.4% of surviving closed-school buildings are in use for something else (MEXT, FY2024 survey).
rev_i6_v: 🔎 Our view: A school is an evacuation site and a place where local events happen. If closure runs ahead of any decision on the buildings, the district is left without that base for a period. The closure dates and the plan for the buildings ought to be shown together.
rev_s12_h: 🎓 Review: the reorganization and the quality of education<small>検証：教育の質から見た再編</small>
rev_s12_lead: The city gives “a better educational environment for children” as the reason for the reorganization. So how will children's learning and growth actually change? Looking at academic ability (understanding and being able to do), personal strengths (relating to others, taking the initiative, taking on challenges) and the conditions behind both (class size, teachers, the transition period, health and safety), we set out what the published material confirms and what it leaves unclear.
rev_k1_h: 1. The educational reason the city gives is “the problems of small schools”
rev_k1_f: 【Fact】The city's New School Development Plan makes “learning together” — children listening to each other and deepening their learning by accepting each other's ideas — the core of its teaching, and says this calls for groups large enough to meet a range of ways of thinking and values. The city's optimal size is 12–24 classes per school for both elementary and junior high (2–4 classes per grade in elementary, 4–8 in junior high), a different range from the national standard of 12–18. In its responses to the public comments, the city accepts that small schools have the advantage of keeping every child in view, and then lists the problems: fewer chances to meet a variety of people, no class reshuffles so relationships become fixed, fewer chances to push each other to grow, and difficulty securing places to shine such as club activities and committees.
rev_k1_v: 🔎 Our view: What is set out are “the problems of today's small schools”. We found no yardstick in the published material for checking what has improved, and by how much, after the reorganization. Nor do the problems the city lists include whether a junior high can have a specialist teacher for every subject (we take this up in the next section).
rev_k2_h: 2. Academic ability: how will “understanding and being able to do” change?
rev_k2_f: 【Fact】Where the city's material touches on academic ability, it is the advantages of the integrated elementary–junior high education being considered for Phase 2 (systematic learning across nine years, easing the stumble on entering junior high, continuing support suited to each child), and the city's recognition that small classes allow close teaching attuned to each child. One public comment said that the claim that integrated education raises academic ability comes with no supporting evidence. At the parents' briefings, some asked whether, with more children, help for those falling behind would be neglected, and others asked for ordinary lessons rather than inquiry lessons to raise academic ability.
rev_k2_v: 🔎 Our view: The published material says neither where the district's children stand academically now nor what the aim is for after the reorganization. Making a school bigger cannot in general be said to raise academic ability in itself; what matters is how small-group teaching, teaching matched to each child's level, and a system for passing records of where a child struggles on to the next grade and school are put in place.
rev_k3_h: 3. Personal strengths: relating to others, taking the initiative, taking on challenges
rev_k3_f: 【Fact】The city explains that each child's abilities grow and social skills develop when children meet a variety of ways of thinking, accept each other, cooperate and push each other to improve. “Learning together” stresses listening to each other without dismissing the other's ideas, and staying beside a child who doesn't understand and explaining in words that get through. At the same time, the city itself lists as a drawback of integrated elementary–junior high education that older elementary pupils get fewer chances, as the oldest in the school, to develop leadership and independence. Komaki City has made a declaration as a “No. 1 City for Children's Dreams and Challenges”.
rev_k3_v: 🔎 Our view: For personal strengths the reorganization cuts both ways. Children will meet more people and have more activities to choose from, but each child's share of roles — committee member, leading a school event, getting to play in a match — may thin out. The published material does not say how the experience of small schools, where every child had some role, will be kept in a large one. The “leadership of older pupils” problem the city itself raised can also arise simply because schools get bigger.
rev_k4_h: 4. Conditions: bigger schools can mean bigger classes
rev_k4_f: 【Fact】The maximum class size (35 in elementary school and the first year of junior high, 40 in the second and third years), the prefectural and national moves to lower it, and the city’s answers in the council are summarized under “Learning and support after the reorganization” on the plan overview page. The city added to the plan that “optimal size” means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and that it has no intention of rejecting small classes. At the briefings, parents spoke of their worry that children used to classes of just over 20 will join classes near the maximum after the reorganization, and asked for smaller classes and assistant homeroom teachers for the first few years.
rev_k4_v: 🔎 Our view: The reorganization increases the number of classes per grade, but in some grades it also increases the number of children per class. We found nothing in the published material on how classes will be formed during the transition, or whether extra teachers will be added. The figure of “about 21–25” given in the council is not far from today's classes of just over 20, but some way from the maximum of 35. How that figure will be kept when classes are formed after the reorganization has not been said.
rev_k5_h: 5. Conditions: learning and wellbeing during the transition
rev_k5_f: 【Fact】Recognizing that a big change of environment can weigh on children's minds and bodies, the city is running exchanges between schools before the reorganization (in elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons and an exchange event in Tokadai Central Park; in junior high, joint satoyama conservation and arts appreciation by Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High). It also states that it will publicize and strengthen the counselling provided by each school's counsellors and school counsellors, pass on information and support methods for children who need support, and maintain special-needs classes and resource-room instruction. The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided; Komaki City Council newsletter).
rev_k5_v: 🔎 Our view: The support arrangements are set out, but we found nothing on how the city will check whether the exchanges are frequent and substantial enough. If Phase 2 goes ahead, some children will see their school environment change twice during compulsory education, and nothing has yet been said about support for them.
rev_k6_h: 6. Conditions: teachers and the content of education decide its quality
rev_k6_f: 【Fact】The city explains that staff numbers will rise as pupil numbers rise with the reorganization, and that it is working with the prefecture so that staff can be placed as planned for FY2027. Under national law (the Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers, Article 7 and others), staff numbers are calculated from the number of classes. Since July 2025 a preparatory research committee has been discussing the new schools' curriculum, educational goals, club activities and so on. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4).
rev_k6_v: 🔎 Our view: What the arrangement with the prefecture involves (how many more teachers, and in what form) and the new schools' curriculum and educational goals do not appear in writing in the published material we could check. They may be written in figures or tables in the briefing materials, but we cannot read the text inside those figures.
rev_k7_h: 7. Conditions: health and safety (school health and medical care)
rev_k7_f: 【Fact】As a heatstroke measure, the city says it is installing bottle-refill water dispensers in every elementary and junior high school for use from summer 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 5). The gyms and grounds of closing schools will be kept from FY2027 onward and are expected to remain designated as evacuation shelters and sites. By law, elementary and junior high schools must have a school nurse-teacher (School Education Act, Articles 37 and 49), and the number is calculated as one for every school with three or more classes, plus one more for elementary schools of 801 or more pupils and junior highs of 751 or more (Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers, Article 8).
rev_k7_v: 🔎 Our view: Going from eight schools to four also means going from eight health rooms to four, and each school nurse-teacher will look after more children. We found nothing in the published material on physical fitness now that bus commuting means less daily walking, or on bus travel and admission at the new schools for children who need medical care.
rev_s13_h: 💡 Ideas: how to grow the abilities children will need, here in this district<small>検討：これからの子どもに要る力を、この地区でどう育てるか</small>
rev_s13_lead: The quality of education is not decided by school size alone. Starting from what the national curriculum asks of each subject, we consider what the reorganization could bring this district's children from eight angles: subject expertise, mathematical ability, the ability to use information, the ability to run a project, the ability to manage a community, and the ability to get through life, everyday life skills and the ability to protect one's health. The 🔎 and 💡 that follow the 【Fact】 are all our own ideas, not something the city is considering.
rev_m_fact_h: What the national curriculum asks of each subject (key points of the Courses of Study)
rev_m_fact_p: 【Fact】The Courses of Study (published in 2017 for both elementary and junior high schools) organize the abilities every subject develops under three pillars — “knowledge and skills”, “thinking, judgement and expression” and “motivation to learn and humanity” — and name language ability, information literacy (including information ethics) and problem-finding and problem-solving ability as the foundation of learning across subjects. Elementary schools also now include learning to think logically through hands-on programming. What all this aims to develop is the “zest for living”. Since FY2022 the national government has also been promoting subject-specialist teaching in the upper elementary grades, with foreign languages, science, mathematics and physical education as the priority subjects (MEXT). The table below is our short summary of each subject's goals.
rev_m_r1_v: Understanding language accurately and expressing oneself appropriately for the listener and the purpose
rev_m_r2_v: Investigating how communities and society work, and thinking and taking part as a member of society
rev_m_r3_v: Thinking mathematically; collecting, reading and making judgements from data (“using data”)
rev_m_r4_v: Observing and experimenting with a plan in mind, and inquiring scientifically
rev_m_r5_v: Communicating through listening, reading, speaking and writing
rev_m_r6_v: Expressing, appreciating and bringing these into daily life
rev_m_r7_v: Enjoying exercise throughout life and keeping mind and body healthy; preventing illness and giving first aid for injuries (including CPR in junior high)
rev_m_r8_v: Engaging with the people, community and nature nearby, and making one's own life better
rev_m_r9_k: Home economics / technology and home economics
rev_m_r9_v: Running one's own life — food, clothing, housing and consumer life; information technology (programming, measurement and control) and more
rev_m_r10_v: Inquiry: setting one's own question, gathering information, organizing and analysing it, and presenting the results
rev_m_r11_v: Taking on a role in a group, deciding things through discussion and carrying them out
rev_m_views_h: 🔎 The reorganization seen through eight abilities
rev_m_v1_p: 🔎 Our view: Because teacher numbers are calculated from the number of classes, the fewer classes a junior high has, the harder it is to have a specialist teacher for every subject (a general point). A bigger junior high directly improves learning in each subject — one of the most concrete advantages of the reorganization. Yet the city's explanation does not put this point forward.
rev_m_v2_p: 🔎 Our view: “Using data” sticks best when it is learned with familiar numbers. This district has real data tied directly to children's own lives — how the number of children has changed, distances to school, how many ride the school bus. Mathematical ability depends less on school size than on what it is taught with.
rev_m_v3_p: 🔎 Our view: Every school has one device per pupil, so information literacy depends less on school size than on how the devices are used. It will not grow automatically with the reorganization. On the other hand, the national guidance also mentions linking distant schools online (Nationwide), which is an option for exchanges before the closures and when thinking about Phase 2.
rev_m_v4_p: 🔎 Our view: The term “project management” does not appear in the Courses of Study, but the cycle in integrated studies and special activities — setting a question, planning, dividing roles, carrying it out and looking back — amounts to it. This ability only grows by actually taking on a role. That large schools tend to leave some children without a role is the same problem as 3 in the previous section.
rev_m_v5_p: 🔎 Our view: Local studies in social studies and the period for integrated studies are where this is learned. This district faces exactly the problems of community management — a falling population, what to do with closing school buildings, commuting and public transport — and the children are themselves among those affected by the reorganization. At the briefings some asked for inquiry learning such as an elementary school's rapeseed-blossom project to be kept, while others wanted ordinary lessons instead of inquiry, so inquiry needs to be shown to connect with academic ability.
rev_m_v6_p: 🔎 Our view: This is the ability to protect one's own life and those around one in disasters and extreme heat. The closed schools will remain as shelters, but children will go every day to a different, more distant school. Knowing the shelter near home, and what to do if disaster strikes on the way to or from school or on the bus, needs to be learned both at school and in the community, but we found nothing on this in the published material.
rev_m_v7_p: 🔎 Our view: This is the “ability to run one's own life” that home economics and life environment studies develop. Children who go by bus will need new independence — moving to a timetable, managing their own belongings, letting someone know on days they won't ride. On the other hand, the chances of meeting local people along the walking route may shrink.
rev_m_v8_p: 🔎 Our view: What is learned in health lessons (health, preventing illness, first aid) and the school health system that supports it are two different things. The former depends little on school size; the latter (health rooms, school nurse-teachers, school doctors, medical care) changes with the number and size of schools (7 in the previous section).
rev_m_ideas_lead: The following are our proposals, not something the city is considering. Each sets out the thinking and what we have not been able to confirm.
rev_m_p1_h: 1. Publish yardsticks for academic ability, personal strengths and conditions in advance, and report on them every year
rev_m_p1_p:
The thinking: No one can say whether the reorganization worked without a yardstick decided in advance. For academic ability, for example: the district-wide trend in the National Assessment of Academic Ability (in a form that identifies no individual or school) and the share of children who say they understand their lessons. For personal strengths: items in the same survey's questionnaire such as “I have good points”, and the share of children who took on a role in committees, events or clubs. For conditions: the number of classes, the grades where classes can be reshuffled, the number of subjects with a specialist teacher, and the number of counselling cases. This also connects to the criteria for deciding whether to go on to Phase 2 (point 4 of “What the plan does not say”).
Not confirmed: how the city intends to check the effects of the reorganization. We have not found this in the published material.
rev_m_p2_h: 2. Protect academic ability: more teachers for the first few years
rev_m_p2_p:
The thinking: The national and prefectural governments have a system for adding teachers (additional staffing) for small-group teaching and teaching by level. Using it generously in the years right after the reorganization, and passing on records of where children struggle across grades and schools, would answer concretely the worries of grades whose classes get bigger. The small schools' strength of “keeping every child in view” can also be kept by having a grade's teachers look after the children together.
Not confirmed: whether staffing for FY2027 includes any additional teachers.
rev_m_p3_h: 3. Link the nine years of inquiry at “Shinooka Gakuen” through “managing the eastern district”
rev_m_p3_p:
The thinking: The city gives continuity of learning across nine years as a reason for considering integrated education. To show that in content, inquiry could take the district's real problems — what to do with the buildings after closure, how the school bus runs, the population outlook — and go deeper as children move up the grades. Investigating a local problem oneself, coming up with ideas and putting them to adults is the very ability to manage a community.
Not confirmed: the new schools' plans for the period for integrated studies.
rev_m_p4_h: 4. Connect mathematics and information through the district's real data
rev_m_p4_p:
The thinking: Using data the city publishes, such as population statistics, combine “using data” in mathematics with “information technology” (programming) in technology. Graphing their own district's numbers, making forecasts and discussing how reliable they are builds mathematical ability and the ability to use information at the same time.
Not confirmed: how devices are currently used at each school.
rev_m_p5_h: 5. Give everyone a role in projects
rev_m_p5_p:
The thinking: Run inquiry projects and events in small teams, with the children themselves handling planning, dividing roles, checking progress and looking back. Mixed-age groups and rotating committee posts mean everyone gets a role even as schools grow. The idea is to build into large schools, by design, what happened naturally in small ones.
Not confirmed: how committees and events will be organized at the new schools.
rev_m_p6_h: 6. Connect children with local adults and places to take on challenges
rev_m_p6_p:
The thinking: Make the eight schools' joint school management council, the eastern-district development initiatives and the community clubs active in the school districts (Community clubs) partners for inquiry and projects. Seeing something through together with adults outside school builds both personal strengths and the ability to manage a community.
Not confirmed: what the school management council will discuss.
rev_m_p7_h: 7. Getting through life: learn disaster preparedness both at school and where children live
rev_m_p7_p:
The thinking: Use the former school buildings, which remain shelters after closure, for community disaster drills and children's disaster education. Children, parents, the bus operator and the community decide together in advance what to do if an earthquake or heavy rain strikes on the way to or from school or on the bus.
Not confirmed: the rules for responding to a disaster while children are on the school bus.
rev_m_p8_h: 8. Everyday life skills: make bus commuting practice in independence
rev_m_p8_p:
The thinking: Hand over things such as moving to a timetable, managing belongings and letting someone know on days they won't ride step by step, starting with what children in each grade can manage. Linked with home economics and life environment studies, the change in how children get to school becomes a chance to build life skills.
Not confirmed: how much of using the bus children are expected to handle themselves.
rev_m_p9_h: 9. Health: judge the school health system by the number of children, not the number of schools
rev_m_p9_p:
The thinking: Before the new schools open, publish the number of school nurse-teachers at each school, the arrangements for school doctors and dentists, and how children who need medical care will be admitted and travel by bus. The Act on Support for Children Requiring Medical Care (2021) makes school founders responsible for giving appropriate support to the children with medical care needs enrolled in their schools. Building fitness to make up for less walking, and measures against extreme heat, also become children's own strengths when combined with health lessons.
Not confirmed: the number of school nurse-teachers at each school after the reorganization, and the arrangements for children who need medical care.
rev_s3_h: 💡 Ideas: how to increase the number of children<small>検討：地区全体の子どもを増やすには</small>
rev_s3_lead: Separately from how schools are arranged, what would it take to increase the number of children in the Shinooka district itself? Everything below is this site’s own proposal; none of it is under consideration by the city.
rev_s3_note: Each item states the thinking it rests on and what we have not been able to confirm. Honestly, at this point there is more in the second column than the first.
rev_p1_h: 1. Publish the assumptions and a target
rev_p1_p:
The thinking: Nobody can work out how much of what would change the outlook without knowing the assumptions behind the projection. If they were published, residents, businesses and the city could argue on the same numbers.
Not confirmed: the assumptions themselves. We could not find them in published material.
rev_p2_h: 2. Help Tokadai New Town turn over to a new generation
rev_p2_p:
The thinking: While the under-19 population has halved, the over-65 population has grown about 2.5 times. In a neighbourhood settled all at once, room for families with children appears as people move on. Tracking empty homes and helping families move into them needs no change to where schools are.
Not confirmed: the number of empty homes, new housing supply, and the age breakdown of the population. These sit with the city’s statistics and planning departments; we have not checked them.
rev_p3_h: 3. Treat the commute as a condition for settling here
rev_p3_p:
The thinking: On school buses, the revised national guidance notes the shortage of drivers and states that it matters to work with the mayoral departments to secure transport for the area as a whole. A child’s school bus and an adult’s commute are two sides of one problem. How easy it is to reach Kasugai — the Tokadai–Torimatsu road and the bus services — bears directly on whether families with children choose this district.
Not confirmed: commuting flows and actual use of public transport in the district. We have not checked them.
rev_p4_h: 4. Make the schools themselves a reason to choose the area
rev_p4_p:
The thinking: The national guidance says that where schools stay small, as much as where they merge, work is needed to draw on the advantages and keep the drawbacks small. Nationwide there are now 232 public compulsory education schools covering all nine years (75,828 pupils, FY2024). The integrated 9-year education being considered for Phase 2 could instead be designed up front as the district’s own character, rather than arriving as a by-product of merging.
Not confirmed: whether Komaki City is considering schemes such as open-enrolment small schools. We have not checked.
rev_p5_h: 5. Use a closing school as a base for families
rev_p5_p:
The thinking: Nationwide, 74.4% of surviving closed-school buildings are in use. If one of the eight closing schools near the centre of the district were given over to childcare support, after-school space and community meeting rooms, it would partly make up for the greater distances that merging brings.
Not confirmed: the condition of each building and what refurbishment would cost. We have not checked.
rev_p6_h: 6. Put the board of education and the mayoral departments in the same room
rev_p6_p:
The thinking: None of items 1–5 can be decided by the board of education alone. The “whole-of-government” pillar of the revised national guidance asks for exactly this: considering schools as a question about the area’s future. Simply adding the housing, transport and childcare departments to the reorganization discussions would widen what can be discussed.
Not confirmed: how the mayoral departments take part in the current process. We have not checked.
rev_p7_h: 7. Examine whether the high school stage could sit in this district
rev_p7_p:
The thinking: There is no high school here; children can stay inside the district up to junior high, but not after that, and the district has lost its university too. While the use of the closing school sites is still open, a school at high school level can still be examined. The next section sets this out in full.
Not confirmed: The conditions of the Shinooka sites, and whether the prefecture and the city have discussed this. This site has not checked.
rev_s10_h: 🏫 Could a high school fit in this district?<small>検討：高校段階をこの地区に置けるか</small>
rev_s10_lead: Phase 2 is about joining elementary and junior high education, but this district has no high school at all. The time when the use of the closing school sites is decided is also the last time this question can be asked.
rev_s10_note: This section does not claim that building a high school would increase the number of children. With a university leaving the district and prefectural high schools being consolidated, putting a high school stage here runs against the current. Even so, once the use of the sites is settled the option disappears altogether — which is why it deserves to be examined once, before that decision.
rev_s11_h: 📡 City Planning Updates (Eastern District)<small>都市計画の動き（東部地域）</small>
rev_tk_lead: The urban planning named in point ③ of the previous section is a tool the city can decide on itself. To see how it is actually moving in the east, we list up to five pages of the city’s Urban Planning Division that mention an eastern place name in their title or text, newest first.
rev_tk_note: 🔄 Checked automatically every day (the whole section once a week). Text inside attached PDFs or figures cannot be read, so something missing here does not mean it was never published. Titles are machine-translated outside Japanese. Fixed dates also go onto the schedule.
rev_h1_h: ① There is no high school in the district
rev_h1_f: 【Fact】Komaki has four high schools: the prefectural Komaki (Komaki 1-chome), Komaki Minami (Ogihigashi) and Komaki Kouka (Kuboisshiki), and the private Homare (Honjo). All of them lie outside the Shinooka district (city facility guide). There is no high school inside the district.
rev_h1_v: 🔎 Our view: Up to junior high, children can reach school inside the district; after that they travel out of it. One public comment said the area suits families raising children but becomes inconvenient from high school onwards. When a family asks how long it can stay here, that step counts.
rev_h2_h: ② Universities and high schools are leaving this area
rev_h2_f: 【Fact】Nagoya University of the Arts moved from Okusa in Komaki to the city of Nagoya in April 2022. At a town meeting held at the Eastern Citizens' Center, the city explained that universities across the country are returning to city centres, moving to well-connected places where students are easier to attract in a time of fewer children; it added that the vacated land belongs to the university, so the city cannot decide its use, but that it strongly hopes for a good one. Aichi Bunkyo University, also in Okusa, has announced that it will stop admitting students from FY2027 (decided at an extraordinary board meeting on 30 March 2026), citing the falling 18-year-old population and years of enrolment below capacity, and says it will provide its teaching and research environment until the current students graduate.Homare High School (Honjo), the city's private high school, has announced on its own site (3 June 2026) that it will move to Minato ward in Nagoya in 2029. The destination is reported to be the site of the former Nagoya racecourse.
rev_h2_v: 🔎 Our view: Before this district can ask whether it could host a high school, it is already losing the places of learning it has. The reasons the universities gave — fewer 18-year-olds, and location — are exactly the conditions any school placed here would run into. So the proposals below are not “invite a school and people will come back”; they are “take these conditions into account when the use of the school sites is decided”.The private high school's move points the same way: schools are gathering where the people are.
rev_h3_h: ③ The moment to decide what the sites are for is now
rev_h3_f: 【Fact】The city says that unless there is a plan to convert a closed school building — one worth its considerable upkeep — the building will in principle be demolished, to hold down costs. Gymnasiums and grounds are to be kept as bases for local sport and disaster response, and the use of the sites is under study by the relevant departments (the city's replies to the public comment and at the parents' briefings). The city also lists Shinooka Elementary among five schools over 60 years old for which a decision must be made soon (New School Development Plan).
rev_h3_v: 🔎 Our view: “Demolition unless there is a plan to convert” means the window for putting a plan forward is limited. Shinooka Elementary and Shinooka Junior High stand where the district's original one-elementary-one-junior-high pair was, but given their age this is a question about the land, not about reusing the present buildings.
rev_h4_h: ④ Three legal forms exist, and one works across different founders
rev_h4_f: 【Fact】Integrated junior/senior high education takes three forms: the secondary school, the attached type in which one founder links a junior high and a high school, and the co-operative type, which works even when the founders differ (School Education Act art. 71; its Enforcement Regulation arts. 75 and 87). In the co-operative type the founder of the junior high agrees the curriculum with the founder of the high school. A municipality establishing a high school or a secondary school needs the approval of the prefectural board of education (School Education Act art. 4), and the prefecture pays staff salaries only up to the lower division of a secondary school (Act on the Salary Burden for Municipal School Staff art. 1).
rev_h4_v: 🔎 Our view: A high school run by the city alone is heavy on both approval and money. The co-operative type, by contrast, can start without a new building, pairing the reorganized junior highs with a prefectural high school in the city. It can be examined before any attempt to attract a school.
rev_h5_h: ⑤ The prefecture is not adding schools — but it has opened a table
rev_h5_f: 【Fact】All ten prefectural integrated schools Aichi has opened are new junior highs attached to existing prefectural high schools; not one is a newly built school. At the same time the prefecture is consolidating its high schools, with junior high graduates expected to fall by about 20% by FY2035; in FY2028 four schools in the Seto area become three. Its Prefectural High School Reorganization Vision states that a forum will be set up for the prefecture and the municipalities to discuss the future of high schools.
rev_h5_v: 🔎 Our view: The prefecture's own documents make plain that asking for a brand-new high school is unlikely to succeed right now. But since the vision itself provides for a forum, there is a way in for telling the prefecture that this district has no high school stage at all.
rev_h6_h: 💡 Proposal 1: Put the high school stage on the list before deciding the sites
rev_h6_p:
The thinking: Once demolition is decided, this can no longer be examined. Simply listing “a school at high school level” among the options for the sites, and costing it once, changes what the decision rests on.
Not confirmed: The area of the Shinooka Elementary and Junior High sites, the state of the buildings, and what conversion would cost. This site has not checked.
rev_h7_h: 💡 Proposal 2: Ask the prefecture for the discussion table
rev_h7_p:
The thinking: Where high schools go is the prefecture's decision. Its vision provides for a forum with the municipalities; setting out that this district has no high school, that it is losing its university, and where its children go after junior high could put the question on that agenda.
Not confirmed: Whether the prefecture and Komaki are already discussing this, and where the district's junior high students go on to. This site has not checked.
rev_h8_h: 💡 Proposal 3: The co-operative type is the quickest to start
rev_h8_p:
The thinking: The co-operative type needs no new building: the reorganized Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi junior highs could begin by linking their curriculum with a prefectural high school in the city. The prefecture already has such pairings, and in April 2026 a prefectural high school working with municipal junior highs joined them. If it works, it is a foothold for whatever comes next.
Not confirmed: Whether the city and the prefecture are considering such a link. This site has not checked.

rev_s5_h: 📊 Review: Did past policies reach the east?<small>検証：これまでの施策は東部に効いたか</small>
rev_s5_lead: The number of children fell, but not because nothing was done here. Over recent decades the city has courted factories, built a new town, expanded childcare support, launched a district development strategy and set up marriage support. Following that record through published material, we ask what worked and what did not, judged on one thing only: the number of children in the eastern district.
rev_src_tobu: Komaki City, Eastern District Development Strategy
rev_y1: Under the factory attraction ordinance (enacted 1956, repealed 1966) the city actively courted factories, and the number of manufacturing establishments rose sharply
rev_y2: The Yokouchi industrial estate, then the Shimozue industrial estate (in the east), are supplied publicly
rev_y3: Residents begin moving into Tokadai New Town, built by Aichi Prefecture as a new residential district development project

rev_y9: Establishments in the eastern district rise from 917 to 1,095 and employees from 12,388 to 20,671. Over the same period the city as a whole falls from 6,970 to 6,654 and from 103,591 to 100,228

rev_y14: A “Meeting and Marriage Support Office” is created in the Children’s Future Department. From that year the city waives nursery fees for children aged 0–2 out of its own budget

rev_e1_h: ① Jobs grew. Children did not
rev_e1_f: 【Fact】Establishments in the eastern district rose from 917 in 2009 to 1,095 in 2014, and employees from 12,388 to 20,671. Over the same period the city as a whole fell from 6,970 to 6,654 establishments and from 103,591 to 100,228 employees (Komaki City, Eastern District Development Strategy). Across the city, 29,416 more people commute in than out, about 55% of them into secondary industry (2020, Komaki City industry status report).
rev_e1_v: 🔎 Our view: The eastern district has succeeded at creating places to work. What did not grow is the district being chosen as a place to live by the people who work there. The question is not how many jobs, but what kind of jobs, and whether the people doing them want to live here.
rev_e2_h: ② Citywide childcare support does not close the gap between districts
rev_e2_f: 【Fact】In 2015 the city declared itself a “No.1 City for Children’s Dreams and Challenges”, and from FY2023 it has waived nursery fees for children aged 0–2 out of its own budget. Yet with 2010 set at 100, district populations in 2018 stood at 106.04 for Komaki-minami and 102.90 for Ajioka, against 88.33 for Shinooka (85.42 for Tokadai). Shinooka’s ageing rate also rose from 15.7% in 2010 to 27.3% in 2018 (Komaki City population vision).
rev_e2_v: 🔎 Our view: These measures apply equally wherever you live in the city. So they may affect whether a family chooses Komaki, but they barely affect which district inside Komaki it chooses. That only the east fell so far suggests the reason was not the cost of raising children.
rev_e3_h: ③ There was essentially only one kind of housing on offer
rev_e3_f: 【Fact】The Tokadai district plan (adopted 19 September 1989, about 322.2 ha) restricts Zone A, which covers most of the area (about 187.9 ha), to detached single-family houses, with a minimum plot of 150 m² and a height limit of 10 m. Zone B, where mid- and high-rise housing is allowed, is about 4.6 ha (Komaki City urban planning). The Eastern District Development Strategy likewise says that “while roads, parks and other infrastructure are well provided, land use in the residential area is restricted.” The east (Shinooka) has 166 vacant buildings, the most in the city.
rev_e3_v: 🔎 Our view: In an estate everyone moves into at once, the children’s generation moves out twenty to thirty years later. For young households to move in at that point, another kind of housing is needed — homes to rent, smaller units, apartments. That the district has the most vacant houses in the city and still no young households is, we think, not because there are too few houses but because there are too few houses of a kind they can move into.
rev_e4_h: ④ The city’s own survey puts transport, not childcare, at the top of the reasons for leaving
rev_e4_f: 【Fact】In the city’s 2018 survey of people moving in and out, people in their 20s to 40s who moved to neighbouring municipalities most often chose their destination because “commuting to work or school is easy” and “public transport is convenient”. What they had been unhappy about in Komaki was, again at the top, “public transport is inconvenient” and “there is a lot of congestion”. Nobody chose “the education environment is good” as a reason for their destination, and nobody named “childcare support” as a source of dissatisfaction with Komaki (Komaki City population vision).
rev_e4_v: 🔎 Our view: The city’s own survey says young households leave over transport, not childcare support. The eastern district lost that transport in 2006 — two years after its population peaked in 2004. We cannot establish cause and effect, but the order of events cannot be ignored.
rev_e5_h: ⑤ Work on marriage and singlehood only began in FY2023
rev_e5_f: 【Fact】The city’s own analysis found that the indicator most strongly correlated with the total fertility rate is the proportion of unmarried women, where Komaki ranks 30th of the 38 cities in Aichi; it ranks 35th for the share of men in regular employment and 32nd for the marital fertility rate. The “Meeting and Marriage Support Office” was created in FY2023, and the contracted marriage support programme and matchmaking subsidy began in FY2024 (Komaki City analysis of declining birthrate).
rev_e5_v: 🔎 Our view: Marriage is the entrance to the birth figures. The dedicated office was created nineteen years after the eastern district’s population peaked, and results there would take another decade or more to show up as pupils in a school. It is not a measure that can arrive in time for the first phase of the reorganization in FY2027.
rev_e6_h: ⑥ Two plans for the same district rest on opposite assumptions
rev_e6_f: 【Fact】The KPI of the Eastern District Development Strategy (FY2022–2031) is the working-age share of the population: the target is to raise the projected 53.0% by one point by FY2026, and the projected 48.7% by two points by FY2031. The school reorganization plan, meanwhile, takes as its premise that by 2033 every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High will have one class per year group.
rev_e6_v: 🔎 Our view: The development plan sets out to move the population structure; the school plan assumes the population will not move. Both are the city’s own plans, for the same district. We could not find, in the published material, any sign that the two have been set against each other in the same forum.
rev_s6_h: 🏛 Who decides, and how far the city’s own powers reach<small>だれが決め、どこまで市が決められるのか</small>
rev_s6_lead: To whom are the six questions above addressed? First each point is matched with the people involved; then come how responsibilities are split inside the city, what lies outside the city’s powers, and the tools the city can use on its own.
rev_r1_h: ① Responsibility is split across five departments or more
rev_r1_f: 【Fact】In the published material, school reorganization sits with the School Reorganization Section of the General Affairs Division of Education; development of the east with the Eastern District Development Promotion Office of the Urban Policy Department; housing and land use with the Urban Planning Division of the same department; childcare and marriage support with the Children’s Future Department (Children’s Policy Division, and the Meeting and Marriage Support Office created in FY2023); business location with the Business Location and Next-Generation Industry Division of the Regional Revitalization Department; and overall coordination with the Secretarial and Policy Division of the Mayor’s Office. Budgets and ordinances go through a vote of the city council.
rev_r1_v: 🔎 Our view: No department in that list holds “the number of children in the eastern district” as its own target. The School Reorganization Section responds to the decline; it is not the section that reverses it, and the measures that might are spread across several departments. In FY2023 the city did assemble a cross-departmental team from six offices to work on the declining birthrate. Whether the same can be done for a place — the east — is the crux.
rev_r2_h: ② What lay outside the city’s powers
rev_r2_f: 【Fact】Tokadai New Town was built by Aichi Prefecture as a new residential district development project. The Tokadai Line was not the city’s own undertaking, and closed in 2006 because of poor performance. Class-size standards and teacher allocation follow national and prefectural rules. The line between the urbanization promotion area and the urbanization control area is drawn by the prefecture, and most of the eastern district outside Tokadai New Town is urbanization control area.
rev_r2_v: 🔎 Our view: Many of the big decisions that gave the east its shape were not the city’s to make alone. That is not the same as saying there was nothing the city could do. As the next card shows, the city has a record of working around exactly these limits.
rev_r3_h: ③ How the city has worked around its limits — and the one tool it has not used
rev_r3_f: 【Fact】Where the national waiver of nursery fees starts at age three, the city has waived fees for children aged 0–2 from FY2023 out of its own budget. Mumps vaccination has been free since October 2011, and Komaki is the only city in Aichi to do this. Marriage support is funded through the national grant for priority measures against the declining birthrate. In May 2021 the city was selected as an “SDGs Future City” by the Cabinet Office. Its designated factory sites are covered by the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme. And both the Tokadai district plan and the location optimization plan are decided by the city itself.
rev_r3_v: 🔎 Our view: There are three ways the city has worked around its limits: ① adding its own top-up to national or prefectural schemes, ② going after national or prefectural grants and designations, and ③ using the planning powers it holds itself. It has a record on ① and ②. It is ③ that is thin. Both the district plan and the location optimization plan are the city’s to decide, yet the housing forms and the guided areas in the east have not moved in response to the district losing more people than any other. The tool that would work best in the east is the one least used.
rev_s7_h: 💡 What should have been done, and what can be worked around now<small>本来どうすべきだったか、これから何を攻略するか</small>
rev_s7_lead: Proposals meant to keep the same oversights from being repeated when the second phase is judged and the closed school buildings are given a use. The city is not considering them.
rev_q1_h: 1. The mix of housing types should have been kept open
rev_q1_p:
The thinking: A district plan of detached houses only, on plots of 150 m² or more, assumes the generation that moved in will simply grow old there. The turnover that inevitably arrives twenty to thirty years after occupation should have been anticipated, with room left for rentable homes and smaller units.
What can be worked around now: the district plan is the city’s to decide. Alongside a way of turning the city’s largest stock of vacant buildings — 166 in the east — into homes young families can move into (renovation support, leasing, splitting into two-household homes), there is room to revisit the rules on use and plot size.
rev_q2_h: 2. When the transport link was lost, housing policy should have been adjusted with it
rev_q2_p:
The thinking: The closure of the Tokadai Line in 2006 changed the premise of the eastern housing estates. As the city’s own survey shows, young households pick their destination first on commuting and public transport. At the moment of closure, the standard of replacement transport should have been fixed as a condition of housing policy.
What can be worked around now: handle the school bus in the same forum as adults’ commuting. The revised national guidance likewise asks municipalities to secure transport for the area as a whole, in cooperation with the mayor’s side of the administration.
rev_q3_h: 3. Settlement support should have been weighted towards the district losing the most people
rev_q3_p:
The thinking: The settlement subsidy and grant apply to the whole city, and as far as we could confirm nothing is weighted towards the east. With Shinooka at 88.33 and Tokadai at 85.42 against 2010, spreading the same money evenly cannot close that gap.
What can be worked around now: add a top-up for the east. The location optimization plan already designates the area around Tokadai Center as a “local hub”, and it is the city that decides how each area is treated.
rev_q4_h: 4. The door to business attraction should have been opened beyond factories and logistics
rev_q4_p:
The thinking: The city’s business location subsidy requires a new or expanded factory of 1,000 m² or more and fixed-asset spending of ¥500 million or more (¥100 million for small and medium enterprises). The five designated factory sites are for factories too. By the city’s own analysis, its industrial structure has an extremely high share of “manufacturing” and “transport and postal services”, while employees per establishment in “information and communications” are considerably below average. Work in IT, design, apparel, music, film and culture reaches neither that floor area nor that level of capital spending. Structurally, there was never a route for such businesses into this district.
What can be worked around now: create a small-scale category measured by people employed and by the business continuing, rather than by floor area and capital spending. The city’s next-generation industry subsidies do include information and communications, but they are for equipment bought by existing small and medium firms in the city — they do not reach small businesses arriving from outside, or people starting out.
rev_q5_h: 5. A town people commute into has to be turned into a town people want to live in
rev_q5_p:
The thinking: 29,416 more people commute in than out, while the age groups that start families show a net outflow. Work here, live elsewhere: that state of affairs has lasted a long time. Living close to work ought to be this district’s strength, and the Eastern District Development Strategy itself calls for “an environment that makes working from home easier”.
What can be worked around now: put workplaces — coworking, satellite offices — into vacant houses and shops in the east, and make them the landing place for the settlement grant’s “new life support for people working in the city”. The scheme already exists; what is missing is somewhere in the east for it to land.
rev_q6_h: 6. The district should have kept a place where cultural and creative work can grow
rev_q6_p:
The thinking: Work in apparel, design, music and film needs neither large floors nor expensive equipment, but it does need cheap workspace and somewhere people gather. The east has peach and grape growing, the Shiki-no-Mori park, 32 parks in all — and eight school buildings about to fall empty. Nationally, 74.4% of surviving closed school buildings are in use for something else (Nationwide).
What can be worked around now: when the use of the closing buildings is decided, put workshops, studios and rehearsal rooms on the list of options from the start. Work that combines local produce with design fits the strategy’s own aim of “creating new appeal from local resources”, and children seeing real work close at hand fits its aim of “an environment in which young people grow attached to the eastern district”.
rev_q7_h: 7. “The number of children in the east” should have been some department’s target
rev_q7_p:
The thinking: In FY2023 the city assembled a cross-departmental team from six offices to work on the declining birthrate. Nothing of the kind exists for the east as a place. The Eastern District Development Strategy’s KPI is the working-age share of the population, not the number of children.
What can be worked around now: put the Eastern District Development Council and the school reorganization review on the same agenda, and adopt the district’s child population as a shared indicator. Then decide which department answers for that figure.
rev_q8_h: 8. Bundle national and prefectural schemes onto one place: the east
rev_q8_p:
The thinking: The city has a record of going out and getting things — topping up nursery fees, free vaccination, marriage support funded by a national grant, selection as a Cabinet Office “SDGs Future City”, designation under the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme. But most of it is aimed at the whole city, and none of it is bundled onto the district losing the most people.
What can be worked around now: layer the housing, transport, work and childcare schemes onto one place. The same money, narrowed to one district, might be enough to change a decision about where to live.

rev_s8_h: 🗾 Review: what the prefecture and the state have done<small>検証：県と国は何をしてきたか</small>
rev_s8_lead: City policy is not the only thing that has moved the population of the eastern district. The new town, and its transport, were both prefectural undertakings, and the wider framework for the falling birthrate is set by the state. Here we look at prefectural and national policy through the same single lens: the number of children in the eastern district.
rev_n1_h: ① National policy on the birthrate has not stopped the fall in births
rev_n1_f: 【Fact】In October 2019 the state made early childhood education and care free (for ages 3–5, and for ages 0–2 in households exempt from residence tax); in April 2023 it created the Children and Families Agency; and in December of that year the Cabinet adopted the “Children’s Future Strategy”, whose “Acceleration Plan” makes FY2024–2026 an intensive period. From October 2024 the income cap on the child allowance was abolished and payment extended to high-school age. Yet in 2024 there were 686,061 births — the first time the figure has fallen below 700,000 since records began in 1899 — and the total fertility rate was 1.15, the lowest ever (Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, vital statistics).
rev_n1_v: 🔎 Our view: These measures matter as ways of easing the burden on households that already have children. But easing that burden has not reversed the fall in births itself. It is the same shape as Komaki’s childcare support failing to bring children back to the east.
rev_n2_h: ② Regional revitalization did not change where people move
rev_n2_f: 【Fact】In 2014 the state enacted the Regional Revitalization Act, setting a target of zero net in-migration to the Tokyo area by 2020. In the government’s own ten-year review, published in 2024, it was accepted that the broad trends of population decline and concentration in the Tokyo area could not be changed. Komaki drew up its population vision and comprehensive strategy under that framework in FY2015, and a second edition in FY2019.
rev_n2_v: 🔎 Our view: Regional revitalization asked every municipality to write a plan, but what decides where people live is work, transport and housing. In the eastern district, as the city’s own survey shows, the reasons for leaving were commuting and public transport. A requirement to write plans did not move any of those three.
rev_n3_h: ③ The prefecture is the party that built the east’s housing and its transport
rev_n3_f: 【Fact】Tokadai New Town was built by Aichi Prefecture as a new residential district development project, and people began moving in in 1980. The Tokadai Line closed in 2006 because of poor performance. The line between the urbanization promotion area and the urbanization control area is also drawn by the prefecture. As birthrate policy the prefecture has adopted the “Aichi Hagumin Plan” and runs a matchmaking support portal, “Aicon Navi”, for people who wish to marry. The city’s designated factory sites are covered by the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme.
rev_n3_v: 🔎 Our view: Ranked by effect, what the prefecture has done to the east is: it built the housing estate, its transport was lost, and it encouraged factories to locate there. Both the prefecture and the city offer childcare and marriage support, but it was the first three that actually moved the population. And we found no mechanism by which the body that built a new town stays with it through the turnover of generations.
rev_n4_h: ④ The state is pursuing smaller classes and fewer schools at the same time
rev_n4_f: 【Fact】In 2021 the state amended the class-size law, lowering the cap for public elementary schools from 40 to 35 over five years. At the same time the standard school size remains 12 to 18 classes, and the guidance revised in August 2026 is built on wider areas, integration and modernization (Nationwide). A further amendment in March 2026 (Act No. 7 of 2026) set the junior high maximum at 35 as well, lowering it grade by grade until FY2027.
rev_n4_v: 🔎 Our view: The 35-pupil cap increases the number of classes at schools where a year group exceeds 35 pupils. Where each year group is below 35, it changes nothing. Of the two national policies running side by side, only the one that merges schools actually bites in Shinooka.
rev_q9_h: 9. The prefecture and the city need a way of seeing an estate through its turnover of generations
rev_q9_p:
The thinking: Aichi Prefecture built Tokadai New Town; Komaki built and has maintained the schools in it. When, forty years after occupation, the children were gone, the clearing-up appeared as the city’s school reorganization. We found no mechanism by which the body that builds a town stays with it for a full cycle.
What can be worked around now: put the renewal of a prefecture-built estate — revisiting permitted uses, supporting people to move house, getting vacant homes onto the market — onto the same table as the city’s Eastern District Development Strategy, and negotiate it with the prefecture. Pulling prefectural schemes into the east is an extension of exactly what the city has already done with grants and designations.
rev_q10_h: 10. Uniform national support needed a way of choosing a place
rev_q10_p:
The thinking: Free early childhood education and the expanded child allowance are available identically anywhere in Japan. So they bear neither on “where in Japan to live” nor on “where in the city to live”. To make them bite in the district losing the most people, something has to be able to choose a place.
What can be worked around now: when the city uses a national or prefectural grant, it can apply with a narrowed target area. It has already done this with the national birthrate grant for marriage support; the same approach could be extended to housing, transport and work.

rev_cv_lead: From everything we have examined, we picked the 10 points that matter most for judging the plan. 【Fact】 marks what rests on published material; 🔎 marks this site’s view.
rev_cv1_h: The assumptions behind “one class per grade by 2033” are not shown
rev_cv1_f: 【Fact】The city expects every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High to have one class per grade by 2033, and says the reorganization cannot wait.
rev_cv1_v: 🔎 Our view: Only the result of the projection is published; how births, moves in and out, and new housing were assumed is not. With the assumptions, residents could separate what cannot be changed from what policy could still change.
rev_cv2_h: No criteria are given for moving on to Phase 2 (one elementary and one junior high school)
rev_cv2_f: 【Fact】Phase 2 — merging into one elementary and one junior high school and introducing integrated elementary–junior high education — is to be considered if numbers fall further after Phase 1, judged by how Phase 1 goes.
rev_cv2_v: 🔎 Our view: What level “falling further” means is not stated. Unless it is said first how Phase 1 will be measured, Phase 2 looks like a foregone conclusion.
rev_cv3_h: The reasons for where the school-route lines are drawn are hard to read
rev_cv3_f: 【Fact】The school bus covers trips of 2 km or more plus areas chosen for local conditions, but Shiroyama 3 and 4-chome are not covered even where the district change makes the trip longer than 2 km. The usage guidelines were to be handed out at briefings, and applications ran from 30 August to 30 September 2026.
rev_cv3_v: 🔎 Our view: The same 2 km can be covered in one case and not in another, and the published materials do not make the reason clear. The application deadline also came before the guidelines were settled.
rev_cv4_h: What happens to the closed school buildings is not set out together with the closure dates
rev_cv4_f: 【Fact】The use of the buildings that will close is left for future consideration in the published materials. Nationally, 74.4% of former school buildings still standing are being used for something else (MEXT survey, FY2024).
rev_cv4_v: 🔎 Our view: Schools are evacuation shelters and venues for local events. If closures go ahead before uses are decided, the area will be without that hub for a while.
rev_cv5_h: Consensus-building is judged by how the process was designed, not by the number of comments
rev_cv5_f: 【Fact】The public comment period drew 142 comments from 55 people. The national guide revised in August 2026 asks both for careful, two-way discussion and for a timeline that does not keep putting off a decision.
rev_cv5_v: 🔎 Our view: Counting comments does not measure support or opposition. What matters is how people were reached, and at which stage what could still be changed.
rev_cv6_h: There is no yardstick for checking whether learning and growth improve after the reorganization
rev_cv6_f: 【Fact】The city says lessons where children learn from each other need a group of a certain size, and lists the problems of small schools (no class reshuffles, few chances to take on roles, and so on). The city’s appropriate size is 12–24 classes per school.
rev_cv6_v: 🔎 Our view: What is shown is “the problems of today’s small schools”. We find no yardstick in the published materials for checking how attainment and personal growth change after the reorganization.
rev_cv7_h: Classes may grow: the state is making classes smaller while merging schools
rev_cv7_f: 【Fact】The class-size cap is 35 for elementary school and the first year of junior high, and junior high is being lowered to 35 step by step until FY2027. Teacher numbers are calculated from the number of classes (Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers). The city says it is not against small classes.
rev_cv7_v: 🔎 Our view: Some year groups used to classes of just over 20 may move into classes near the cap. Here, where every grade is below 35, only the merging half of the state’s two policies has any effect. Whether extra teachers will be added for the transition years has not been said.
rev_cv8_h: Support for children’s wellbeing in the transition, and for health and safety, is not yet visible
rev_cv8_f: 【Fact】The city sets out exchanges between schools before the merger, stronger counselling and handing on information about children who need support. School nurses are allotted basically one per school of three or more classes, and the gyms and grounds of closing schools are to stay as evacuation sites.
rev_cv8_v: 🔎 Our view: Going from eight schools to four also means going from eight nurse’s offices to four. How the exchanges will be judged sufficient, bus travel and admission for children needing medical care, and preparing for the school and the home evacuation site being different are not in the published materials.
rev_cv9_h: Jobs increased, but children did not
rev_cv9_f: 【Fact】Establishments in the eastern district rose from 917 in 2009 to 1,095 in 2014, and employees from 12,388 to 20,671 (Eastern District Development Strategy). Meanwhile the district’s under-20 population is less than half of what it was 20 years ago. Most of Tokadai is zoned for detached houses only, and the Tokadai Line closed in 2006.
rev_cv9_v: 🔎 Our view: Child-rearing support that is the same anywhere in the city does little to decide which district people live in. We think the bigger factors were the lack of housing young households can move into and of ways to commute.
rev_cv10_h: No department has “the number of children in the east” as its goal, and the tools the city can decide on itself go unused
rev_cv10_f: 【Fact】Responsibility is split: school reorganization lies with the Board of Education, eastern development and land use with the Urban Policy Department, child-rearing with the Children’s Future Department, and business location with the Regional Revitalization Department. The Tokadai district plan and the location optimization plan are plans the city decides itself. The revised national guide asks for planning together with town development, including the mayor’s departments.
rev_cv10_v: 🔎 Our view: The school reorganization section deals with the result of decline; it is not there to increase numbers. In our view, the urban-planning tools that would help the east most are the ones least used.
rev_cp_lead: These are this site’s proposals, not something the city is considering. The evidence for each, and what we have not been able to confirm, can be read via “More” on the In-depth page.
rev_cp_g1: Protect and raise the quality of education
rev_cp_g2: Increase the number of children in the east
rev_cp1_h: Publish the yardsticks for learning first, and report every year
rev_cp1_p: 💡 Proposal: Before the reorganization, publish measures of attainment (such as the share of children who say they understand lessons, in a form that identifies no person or school), personal growth (such as the share who took on a role) and conditions (number of classes, grades where classes can be reshuffled, subjects with specialist teachers), and report on them every year. These can also serve as the criteria for Phase 2.
rev_cp2_h: Add teachers for the transition years
rev_cp2_p: 💡 Proposal: Use the national and prefectural extra-teacher allocations heavily in the first years after the merger, combining small-group and ability-based teaching with passing on records of where children struggle. This answers concretely the worries of year groups whose classes get bigger.
rev_cp3_h: Link nine years of inquiry learning with the district’s real issues and data
rev_cp3_p: 💡 Proposal: Take the district’s own issues — the use of closed buildings, the bus service, the population outlook — and combine lessons that graph the city’s statistics and make forecasts, projects where every child takes a role, and chances to try things with local adults. This builds maths, information skills and the ability to run a community together.
rev_cp4_h: Turn bus travel and disaster preparedness into lessons in independence and resilience
rev_cp4_p: 💡 Proposal: Hand children tasks suited to their grade, such as moving to the timetable and reporting days they will not ride. In the former school buildings kept as shelters, children, parents, the bus operator and the community draw up the disaster rules together.
rev_cp5_h: Plan health support by the number of children, not the number of schools
rev_cp5_p: 💡 Proposal: Before the new schools open, publish the number of school nurses at each, the school-doctor arrangements, and how children needing medical care will be admitted and travel by bus. Link fitness to make up for less walking, and heat measures, with health lessons.
rev_cp6_h: Publish the assumptions and targets, and make the number of children in the east a department’s goal
rev_cp6_p: 💡 Proposal: With the assumptions public, residents, businesses and the city can argue from the same figures. Put the eastern development council and the school reorganization discussions in the same forum, adopt the east’s child population as a shared indicator, and decide which department is responsible for it.
rev_cp7_h: Mix housing types as the new town changes generations
rev_cp7_p: 💡 Proposal: Review the district plan of detached houses only on plots of 150 m² or more, and turn the 166 vacant homes — the most in the city — into homes that families with children can move into, through renovation support and leasing. The prefecture and city should discuss regenerating the housing area the prefecture built within one framework.
rev_cp8_h: Treat commuting and school travel as a condition for settling
rev_cp8_p: 💡 Proposal: Children’s school buses and adults’ commutes are two sides of the same problem. In the city’s own survey, transport was among the top reasons young households gave for choosing where they moved. Consider roads and bus routes toward Kasugai and elsewhere together with housing policy.
rev_cp9_h: Make closing school sites hubs for families, and keep a high school stage as an option
rev_cp9_p: 💡 Proposal: Use the buildings nearest the district’s centre for child-rearing support, after-school places and meeting space, making up for schools being further away. Before deciding on demolition, estimate once the conditions and costs of a high school stage as an option.
rev_cp10_h: Open doors for work other than factories and logistics, turning a “place to work” into a “place to live”
rev_cp10_p: 💡 Proposal: The city’s business-location subsidy requires at least 1,000 m² of floor space and 500 million yen of investment (100 million for SMEs), which IT, design and cultural work cannot reach. Create a small scheme measured by jobs, and workspaces in vacant homes and shops in the east, as a landing place for the settlement grant for people working in the city.

rev_pt_gaps: 🔎 In short: On six points — the projection’s assumptions, efforts to increase children, the school-route lines, the criteria for Phase 2, consensus-building and the closed buildings — the published materials do not provide what is needed to judge.
rev_pt_power: 🔎 In short: Most of the six questions cannot be answered by the Board of Education alone. No department has the number of children in the east as its goal, and the urban-planning tools the city can decide on itself are the least used.
rev_pt_quality: 🔎 In short: The city shows “the problems of today’s small schools”, but there is no yardstick yet for checking whether learning and growth improve afterwards. Little has been published on class size, teachers, the transition period, or health and safety.
rev_pt_skills: 💡 In short: Starting from the skills the national curriculum asks for in each subject, we look at the reorganization through eight abilities and make nine proposals for developing them here.
rev_pt_history: 🔎 In short: Factory attraction and industrial estates added jobs, but not children. What did not work was child-rearing support that is the same across the city; what was missing was the right types of housing and transport.
rev_pt_nation: 🔎 In short: The prefecture built the new town and its transport. National birth-rate measures and regional revitalization have not changed the trend. The state is making classes smaller while merging schools, but only the latter affects this district.
rev_pt_should: 💡 In short: Ten proposals, on housing types, transport, settlement support, entry points for work and responsible departments, so that past oversights are not repeated.
rev_pt_ideas: 💡 In short: Seven proposals for increasing the number of children in the whole district, separate from where the schools go.
rev_pt_highschool: 💡 In short: There is no high school in this district. With five facts and three proposals, we look at keeping a high school stage as an option before the use of the school sites is decided.
